excerpt.locator: Wormwood Scrubbs; complete poem, opening “Wormwood scrubs, Wormwood scrubs”, closing “She'll never get it clean!”.

questions.prompt: How does the cleaning job grow larger as the poem goes on?
facilitatorNotes: It starts with household surfaces and containers, then expands to public seats, city halls, streets, and Saint Paul’s. Ask the child to contrast one small object with one large place.
evidence: Pots and pans and pickle-tubs,
Wormwood scrubs the London streets,

questions.prompt: What do the repeated words “Wormwood scrubs” make you imagine about her movement?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition can sound like repeated back-and-forth strokes or endless work. Accept an alternative rhythm-based description tied to the recurring action.
evidence: Wormwood scrubs, Wormwood scrubs

questions.prompt: Does the poem think working even harder will finish the job? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: No: even a ton of effort will never get it clean. The enormous task and emphatic ending suggest impossibility, not laziness.
evidence: Though she use a ton of elbow-grease
She'll never get it clean!

days.title: Hopsy Upsy
days.challenge: Follow a practical sequence through extravagant images.
days.focus: An ordinary bath becomes a sparkling imagined landscape.
days.context: This is a grown-up’s song to a baby during washing and dressing.

excerpt.locator:
Hopsy Upsy; source blocks 475–480, beginning “Hopsy upsy, Baby oh!
Into your bath you now must go;
Splash and dash, and paddle and plash” and ending “ as silver they fall and flow.
Now toss him up and carry him down,
The bonniest Baby in Boston town!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 114.

questions.prompt: Which object signals that the bath is ending?
facilitatorNotes: The towel follows soap and bubbles, then clothes and curls finish the routine.
evidence: Here is the towel for Baby oh!

questions.prompt: What are the “Rainbow isles” really?
facilitatorNotes: Soap bubbles seem like little rainbow islands floating in foam. Ask what colors and shapes make the image work.
evidence: Rainbow isles in a sea of foam,

questions.prompt: How do “scrub and rub, and rub and scrub” help someone perform the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The reversed repeated words create a back-and-forth rhythm that fits drying the baby.
evidence: Now scrub and rub, and rub and scrub,

days.title: Barn Swallow — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice how movement words do work that colour description cannot.
days.focus: A portrait admits the limits of words while vividly describing flight.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. The author is describing an American swallow and distinguishes it from a European relative. Gyrating means circling; a rafter is a beam supporting a roof.

excerpt.locator: Barn Swallow entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “Any one who attempts to describe the coloring of a bird's plumage knows how inadequate wor” and ending “usly spotted with brown and lilac that were all too familiar in the marauding days of our childhood.”.

questions.prompt: The author says the bird is hard to describe. Which movement words nevertheless help you see it?
facilitatorNotes: Wheeling, skimming, darting and gliding offer different motions. Invite the child to choose two and explain their difference rather than merely repeat a list.
evidence: gyrating, darting, and gliding through the air

questions.prompt: Why call the swallow a bird of the air even when it is sitting on a wire?
facilitatorNotes: The perch is temporary; sudden flight returns it to what the author calls its true element. The electrical-shock comparison makes the departure seem quick.
evidence: suddenly it darts off as if it had received a shock of electricity

questions.prompt: What combination of materials and location makes the nest different from a twig nest in a tree?
facilitatorNotes: Mud or clay mixed with straw forms a bracket-like structure under rafters or a bridge arch. Mention both construction and placement.
evidence: these swallows build their bracket-like nests of clay or mud pellets intermixed with straw.

days.title: The Brownies On Roller Skates — Watching the rink (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hear a character build a case by listing earlier adventures.
days.focus: A new desire grows from both sound and spectacle.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have reached town and are looking for the skating hall. They observe from its roof and plan to enter after people leave; the actual skating follows outside this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES ON ROLLER SKATES. Text blocks 6–11; opening “Now, guided by the rumbling sound”; closing “We may command when set on wheels."”.

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies find the skating hall before they can see its floor?
facilitatorNotes: They follow the rumbling sound through the streets. It is a useful sound clue rather than a map or sign.
evidence: Now, guided by the rumbling sound

questions.prompt: Why does one Brownie mention flying, ocean surf, and coasting?
facilitatorNotes: He lists other pleasures to show how much he still wants this new one; skating would “crown” his experiences.
evidence: On roller skates would crown it all.

questions.prompt: Why does the leader choose to wait an hour?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the humans to leave and the hall to become available for the secretive Brownies. The plan depends on timing.
evidence: Will quit their sport and homeward go;

days.title: The Brownies At Lawn-Tennis
days.challenge: Hear the difference between careful preparation and disorderly play.
days.focus: Tennis vocabulary makes the game sound orderly before the Brownies bend its rules.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. Tennis uses rackets, a net, marked courts, and special scoring calls such as deuce. Children need not master scoring to notice the contrast.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AT LAWN-TENNIS. Text blocks 1–5; opening “ONE evening as the woods grew dark,”; closing “And Brownies all must disappear.”.

questions.prompt: What corrects the first guess about what is stored in the little building?
facilitatorNotes: Another Brownie identifies tennis equipment and describes the nearby court and its daytime players.
evidence: The fixtures for the tennis ground.

questions.prompt: Which preparations show that they know a court needs more than a ball and rackets?
facilitatorNotes: They set posts and mark service lines, baselines and courts. Invite two details rather than a full equipment list.
evidence: With service-line and line of base,

questions.prompt: How does the number of players turn an orderly game into a crowded joke?
facilitatorNotes: A dozen join where four should stand; tangles and wrong positions follow, but they keep playing.
evidence: And in the game where four should stand,
At least a dozen took a hand.

days.title: Saint John's Wood
days.challenge: Compare the leafy place described first with the changed place at the end.
days.focus: Green-to-grey contrast makes a playful place-name poem feel wistful.
days.context: Saint John’s Wood is a London place name. Farjeon imagines a figure living among animals and trees; this is poetic invention, not a documented account of a saint’s life. A haunch is the upper part of an animal’s back leg.

excerpt.locator: Saint John's Wood; complete poem, opening “Saint John walked in a Wood”, closing “But where's the good Saint John?”.

questions.prompt: Which creatures make the first Wood seem alive? Choose two and say what they do.
facilitatorNotes: Squirrels climb, pigeons coo, and hares sit on their haunches. The different motions and sound fill the wood with life.
evidence: And Squirrels climbed and Pigeons cooed.
And Hares sat on their haunches.

questions.prompt: How do the willow huts and hazel-nuts connect Saint John to the Wood?
facilitatorNotes: He finds shelter and food in its plants. Invite the child to connect each detail to a need, rather than making unsupported claims about his whole life.
evidence: He built him willow huts
His meat was chiefly hazel-nuts,

questions.prompt: Why might the final question feel different from the cheerful opening?
facilitatorNotes: The Wood changes from green to grey, and the person is missing. Children may hear sadness, curiosity, or surprise; support the feeling with the change and question.
evidence:
His Wood that grew so green
Is now as grey as stone;
But where's the good Saint John?

days.title: The Fairies
days.challenge: Revise a first interpretation when a second speaker offers clues.
days.focus: A mother uses fairy language to reveal her delight in children.
days.context: The first five verses are the child’s questions. The next five are the mother’s reply; change voices at “True it is.”
days.contentNote: The closing blessing expresses the mother’s religious language.

excerpt.locator:
The Fairies; source blocks 203–212, beginning “Is it true, my mother?
Can it really be,
That the little fairies
Every day you see?
Oh! th” and ending “ook into the glass, dear!
One of them you'll see.
Oh! the little fairies,
God bless them all for me!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 56, 57, 58, 59.

questions.prompt: Where does the child imagine the fairies might live?
facilitatorNotes: Garden, meadow, brookside, woodland, and a rose palace are possibilities; the mother will redirect this search indoors.
evidence: Is it by the brookside,

questions.prompt: Which actions begin to reveal what the mother means by fairies?
facilitatorNotes: Peeping, tugging her apron, climbing into her lap, and tumbling down describe playful children.
evidence: Tugging at my apron,

questions.prompt: Why does the mother tell the child to look in the glass?
facilitatorNotes: A mirror will show the child as one of the “fairies.” This gives the riddle’s answer rather than showing a separate magical creature.
evidence: Look into the glass, dear!

days.title: Cedar Bird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate observable actions from the human manners the writer imagines.
days.focus: Quiet flock behaviour becomes a portrait of elaborate politeness.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. Cedar bird is a name used here for the cedar waxwing. Gregarious means living in groups; gormandized means eaten heartily. This excerpt begins with the flock’s quiet voices.

excerpt.locator: Cedar Bird entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “One listens in vain for a song; only a lisping "Twee-twee-ze," or "a dreary whisper," as M” and ending “e never guilty of jolting or crowding. Few birds care to take life so easily, not to say indolently.”.

questions.prompt: What would a listener hear instead of a full song?
facilitatorNotes: A low lisping or whispering call. The lack of loud song suits the description of birds resting high in trees after feeding.
evidence: only a lisping "Twee-twee-ze,"

questions.prompt: What actual action leads Nuttall to call the birds excessively polite?
facilitatorNotes: They pass a worm along a row and back before it is eaten. Discuss the observed passing separately from the imagined human motive of politeness.
evidence: passing a worm from one to another down a whole row of beaks and back again

questions.prompt: When does the flock stop behaving like one large social company?
facilitatorNotes: At nesting time it breaks into pairs. The author shifts from flock manners to the work and intimacy of nesting.
evidence: they give up their gregarious habits and live in pairs

days.title: The Brownies At The Seaside — At the water’s edge (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare different swimmers’ choices and the group’s shared limit.
days.focus: Individual confidence varies within one joyful crowd.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have reached the beach and put on bathing clothes. This closing passage describes their swim and return plan. The activities belong to a fantasy, not a swimming lesson.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AT THE SEASIDE. Text blocks 11–15; opening “Then, when a boat was manned with care”; closing “To sport in rolling surf again.”.

questions.prompt: Why do they put watchers in a boat before the swimming starts?
facilitatorNotes: The boat watches for overbold swimmers who may suffer cramp or cold. It shows concern about trouble even in this playful scene.
evidence: To watch for daring swimmers there,--

questions.prompt: Do all the Brownies choose to leap into deep water?
facilitatorNotes: No: some creep in, and others stay in shallow surf holding aid lines. The scene contains different comfort levels.
evidence:
While others were content to stay
In shallow surf, to duck and play

questions.prompt: What two plans do they keep in mind while enjoying the waves?
facilitatorNotes: They must get home before sunrise, yet they also promise to return each warm summer. The immediate departure does not end their love of the beach.
evidence: And kept in mind their homeward race
That every year, when summer's glow

days.title: The Brownies At The Gymnasium — A contest without a winner (excerpt)
days.challenge: Track changes from individual tricks to a group tug-of-war.
days.focus: Exaggerated acrobatics lead to a comic contest that daylight must finish.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have found a gym and are choosing activities. Their magical feats and impossible escapes are fantasy.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AT THE GYMNASIUM. Text blocks 5–10; opening “"For clubs," a second answered there,”; closing “Soon made them drop the rope and run.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask for a bar or ring instead of heavy weights?
facilitatorNotes: He prefers swinging and turning to lifting; he imagines outdoing a monkey on a vine.
evidence: But give me bar or give me ring,

questions.prompt: How does the tug-of-war spread beyond one sensible playing place?
facilitatorNotes: It travels over furniture and up and down stairs; that moving setting helps explain the falls and torn coats.
evidence: Then up and down the winding stairs,

questions.prompt: Who or what finally settles the contest: the judge, a stronger team, or something else?
facilitatorNotes: Neither team wins and the judge cannot decide. Sunrise forces both to drop the rope and flee.
evidence: Soon made them drop the rope and run.

days.title: Ladywell
days.challenge: Hear “well” shift from a place to a question about feeling well.
days.focus: A tiny accident-and-rescue story becomes a punning conversation.
days.context: A well is a deep hole used to reach water. Here a make-believe rescue uses a crooked pin, like a comic fishing hook. The poem is playful; nobody should sit on the edge of a real well.
days.contentNote: A brief, comic fall into a well ends in rescue; the context distinguishes fantasy from safe behaviour.

excerpt.locator: Ladywell; complete poem, opening “The Lady sat”, closing “You are certain to spill."”.

questions.prompt: What causes the fall, and what happens before the Lady speaks?
facilitatorNotes: She loses her balance; others fish her up with a crooked pin. The order matters: she is already rescued when she answers.
evidence:
She lost her balance
And in she fell!

They fished her up
With a crooked pin;

questions.prompt: How can “Well, Lady, well?” ask more than where the Lady has been?
facilitatorNotes: It can ask whether she is well after falling into a well. Her answer “very ill” makes the health meaning clear.
evidence: "Well, Lady, well?"
"Sir, very ill!

questions.prompt: Why is “She came out wetter / Than she went in” a funny way to describe the rescue?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison calmly states an obvious result of falling into water. Children may notice its understatement after the sudden accident.
evidence:
She came out wetter
Than she went in.

days.title: The Queen Bee — three acts of protection (part 1)
days.challenge: Hear the repeated refusal and remember the three kinds of creature it protects.
days.focus: A character dismissed as foolish notices vulnerable lives.
days.context: Three brothers travel together; the youngest is called Witling, an unkind nickname suggesting foolishness.
days.contentNote: The brothers propose harming animals; Witling prevents it. The nickname is presented as the brothers’ judgment, not a label to use for people.

excerpt.locator: The Queen Bee — three acts of protection (part 1); source blocks 2517–2522; begins “THE QUEEN BEE”; ends “"Leave the little creatures alone, I will not suffer them to be stifled."”.

questions.prompt: How do the older brothers’ first words about Witling differ from what his actions show?
facilitatorNotes: They jeer at his simplicity, but he repeatedly notices harm and prevents it. Do not require a claim that he is clever at everything.
evidence: they jeered at his simplicity

questions.prompt: What changes in Witling’s repeated sentences as the danger to each animal changes?
facilitatorNotes: He prevents disturbance of ants, killing of ducks and stifling of bees. Reread the verbs to show a repeated form adapted to each danger.
evidence: I will not suffer them to be stifled.

questions.prompt: Why is the honey’s overflowing detail important to understanding the older brothers’ plan?
facilitatorNotes: It explains what tempts them: they want the honey and propose smoke to obtain it. The listener can separate wanting food from the harmful method.
evidence: it overflowed and ran down the trunk

days.title: The Queen Bee — creatures return the help (part 2)
days.challenge: Match each earlier protected creature to a different task and its special ability.
days.focus: Earlier choices become useful relationships rather than forgotten episodes.
days.context: Witling has protected ants, ducks and bees from his brothers. The travellers reach an enchanted castle.
days.contentNote: Two brothers are magically turned to stone and later restored. The ending treats princesses as marriage prizes, a historical fairy-tale convention to discuss as fiction.

excerpt.locator: The Queen Bee — creatures return the help (part 2); source blocks 2523–2527; begins “At last the three brothers came to a castle where there were in the stables many horses st”; ends “became king after her father's death. But his two brothers had to put up with the two other sisters.”.

questions.prompt: Why can five thousand ants succeed where the two older brothers fail?
facilitatorNotes: The many small searchers can work through moss and gather scattered pearls. The precise count suggests abundance and cooperation, not one unusually strong ant.
evidence: five thousand ants

questions.prompt: How does the queen-bee identify the youngest princess when looking at the three faces is no help?
facilitatorNotes: The princesses look alike but have eaten different sweets. The bee detects the honey and settles on that princess’s lips.
evidence: settled on those of the one that had eaten honey

questions.prompt: What does the final awakening change about the earlier threat of turning into stone?
facilitatorNotes: The threat is real within the tale, but the spell can be undone: everyone regains their own form at the end.
evidence: every one awoke from stony sleep

days.title: The Force of Need
days.challenge: Compare a narrator’s final judgment with the actual dialogue.
days.focus: A robin’s changing circumstances test how we judge an earlier refusal.
days.context: Listen to the offered bread in warm weather and again in winter. The robin answers differently as its circumstances change.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “THE FORCE OF NEED”, beginning “"Hey, Robin! ho, Robin!
  Singing on the tree,
I will give you white b”, ending “ _you_ ever chanced to see
One beg for crust that sneered at crumb
  In bright prosperity?”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 134.

questions.prompt: What does the robin already have when it first refuses bread?
facilitatorNotes: Warmth, grass, a singing breeze, and a waiting mate give it reasons to remain outside.
evidence: the sun is warm and bright;

questions.prompt: Which winter details explain the changed answer?
facilitatorNotes: Raw wind, dead flowers, frost, and a wish for warmth make the offer useful now.
evidence: The frost is on the thorn,

questions.prompt: Does the robin really “sneer” when it first declines?
facilitatorNotes: Its words call the offer kindly courtesy, so the narrator’s final description is harsher than the dialogue. Children may challenge that mismatch with evidence.
evidence: Your kindly courtesy.

days.title: King Alfred and the Cakes
days.challenge: Distinguish what a character knows from what the narrator tells us.
days.focus: A king’s important worries do not prevent a small everyday failure.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.
days.contentNote: War is the background, and an uncertain report says the woman struck Alfred. The narrator’s sweeping insult toward the Danes is a historical stereotype, not a description of Danish people.

excerpt.locator: King Alfred and the Cakes; source blocks 16–28, beginning “Many years ago there lived in Eng-land a wise and good king whose name was Al-fred. No oth” and ending “ny days until he had gath-ered his men to-geth-er again, and had beaten the Danes in a great battle.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the woman expect Alfred to watch the cakes?
facilitatorNotes: She gives a hungry stranger a simple task in return for food and shelter; she does not know his rank.
evidence: She had no thought that he was the king.

questions.prompt: Does he neglect the cakes because he refuses to work?
facilitatorNotes: The woman thinks so, but the narrator says he is absorbed in plans for his army. Knowing the reason does not undo the burnt food.
evidence: His mind was busy making plans for to-mor-row.

questions.prompt: Where does the narrator admit uncertainty?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator doubts the report of a beating and does not know whether Alfred ate supper. Such phrases help distinguish a story’s guesses from definite claims.
evidence: I do not know whether he had any-thing to eat that night,

days.title: Three Fortunes
days.challenge: Compare three versions of what counts as good fortune.
days.focus: A promised magic prize competes with opportunities encountered along the way.
days.context: The three travelers look for a purse where a rainbow touches the ground. “Jocund” means cheerful.
days.contentNote: The two successful fortunes are framed through men finding women and settling down, reflecting the poem’s narrow nineteenth-century social assumptions.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “THREE FORTUNES”, beginning “    A merry young shoemaker,
    And a tailor, and a baker,
Went to se”, ending “ the luck that may
    Chance to fall within his way,
Than to toil for an imaginary thing.”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 42.

questions.prompt: What are the travelers hoping the purse will do?
facilitatorNotes: It should stay full of gold; the goal is a magical promise, not a known destination.
evidence: always full of gold.

questions.prompt: Why do the shoemaker and tailor stop before finding it?
facilitatorNotes: Each finds companionship or a comfortable life worth choosing now; neither reaches the original goal.
evidence: and here I'll stay.

questions.prompt: Is the poem saying all difficult goals should be abandoned?
facilitatorNotes: Its target is an imaginary prize pursued while real opportunities are ignored. The baker’s endless wandering matters to interpreting that limit.
evidence: Than to toil for an imaginary thing.

days.title: Hans in Luck, part 1: gold for a horse, a horse for a cow
days.challenge: Compare what Hans actually has with the advantages he imagines having.
days.focus: The same object can look valuable or burdensome depending on a character’s attention.
days.context: Hans has finished seven years of service and is walking home to his mother with his wages. This is the first of five nights reading the whole tale.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Hans in Luck", opening through the horse-for-cow exchange; begins “HANS IN LUCK”; ends “the peasant, swinging himself into the saddle, was soon out of sight.”

questions.prompt: Which two details show that the gold is both a generous reward and an awkward thing to carry?
facilitatorNotes: His master praises faithful service and gives a head-sized lump; Hans complains that its weight hurts his shoulder. Both views can be true.
evidence: it hurts my shoulder

questions.prompt: Why does Hans compare riding with sitting in an arm-chair?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines comfort and ease, ignoring what he does not yet know about controlling a horse. Ask what that cosy comparison leaves out.
evidence: sitting as much at one's ease as in an arm-chair

questions.prompt: What happens the first time Hans tries to make the horse go fast, and whom does he blame?
facilitatorNotes: He clicks his tongue and cries “Gee-up!” as he was told, and is thrown into the ditch. He blames the horse, calling it a jade, and decides riding is poor work. Some children say the horse really was wild; the text says only that it began to trot.
evidence: Hans was thrown before he knew what was going to happen
Poor work, riding

questions.prompt: Who first suggests trading the horse for the cow, and why does the peasant call the trade a favour?
facilitatorNotes: Hans praises the cow and wishes aloud for one; only then does the peasant offer to exchange, “since it will be doing you such a favour.” Some listeners suspect the peasant is glad to get a horse, pointing to how quickly he rides out of sight; others take him at his word.
evidence: What would I not give to have such a cow!
since it will be doing you such a favour

days.title: Hans in Luck, part 2: a cow for a pig
days.challenge: Compare what Hans expects from each new possession with what actually happens.
days.focus: Each disappointment is followed at once by a new wish, which keeps the chain of trades moving.
days.context: Recap: Hans traded his lump of gold for a horse. When the horse threw him into a ditch, he traded it for a peasant’s cow.
days.contentNote: The cow kicks Hans on the head and he lies dazed until a butcher helps him up. The butcher speaks plainly about killing animals for meat.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Hans in Luck", from the cow trade through the cow-for-pig exchange; begins “And Hans went along driving his cow quietly before him, and thinking”; ends “who was turned out of his wheelbarrow and was to be led by a string.”

questions.prompt: What does Hans expect his cow to give him, and what happens when he tries to milk her?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines butter, cheese and milk whenever he is thirsty; no milk comes, and the cow kicks him. The gap between plan and result repeats what happened with the horse.
evidence: if I am thirsty I have nothing to do but to milk my cow
but not a drop came

questions.prompt: Hans eats all his food and spends his last two farthings at the inn. Why might the storyteller tell us this just before the hot heath?
facilitatorNotes: He now has nothing left, so his thirst on the heath matters. It also shows him enjoying the moment without planning. Some children call this careless, others happy; both fit the words “in the joy of his heart.”
evidence: bought half a glass of beer with his last two farthings

questions.prompt: How does the butcher explain the dry cow, and how quickly does Hans change what he wants?
facilitatorNotes: The butcher says she is old and only fit to pull loads or to be slaughtered. Hans at once decides cow beef is tasteless and wishes for a young pig and sausages: each new thing becomes the thing he always wanted.
evidence: she is old and only fit to draw burdens
Now, if I had but a young pig

questions.prompt: The butcher says he will exchange “just for love of you.” Do you believe him? Which details help you decide?
facilitatorNotes: He had just called the cow fit only to draw burdens or be slaughtered, yet he takes her gladly; some children decide he got the better bargain. Others take him at his word. Hans, who cries “Heaven reward such kindness!”, does not question him at all.
evidence: just for love of you I will exchange
Heaven reward such kindness!

days.title: Hans in Luck, part 3: the worrying pig
days.challenge: Notice the difference between a stranger’s warning and evidence that proves the warning.
days.focus: Fear makes an exchange feel like a rescue.
days.context: Recap: Hans has traded his gold for a horse, the horse for a cow, and the cow for a young pig, which he leads on a string. A young man carrying a goose joins him on the road.
days.contentNote: The passage mentions roasting farm animals and a threat of imprisonment; it contains no injury scene.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Hans in Luck", part 3 of five contiguous nights; begins “So on went Hans, thinking how everything turned out according to his”; ends “I shall sleep upon it, and how pleased my mother will be!"”

questions.prompt: Does the peasant show that Hans’s pig really is the stolen one?
facilitatorNotes: No. He says a pig was stolen and that he fears Hans has it, but supplies no identifying proof. Children may notice that his cautious glances make the warning sound convincing.
evidence: I fear, I fear you have it in your hand

questions.prompt: What makes Hans want the goose before the two men have agreed on a trade?
facilitatorNotes: He first admires its weight, then becomes frightened that keeping the pig will get him into trouble. The immediate cause of his request is fear.
evidence: Poor Hans grew pale with fright.

questions.prompt: Why does Hans list roast goose, fat and feathers at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He tells himself the exchange supplies several useful things and imagines his mother’s pleasure. His optimistic list helps him feel fortunate even though the warning was unproved.
evidence: first I get the roast goose; then the fat

days.title: Hans in Luck, part 4: the grinder’s promise
days.challenge: Follow a chain of remembered exchanges told backwards through short questions.
days.focus: An attractive promise can hide the work needed to make it come true.
days.context: Recap: frightened that his pig might be a stolen one, Hans has traded it for a goose. Now he reaches the last village before home.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Hans in Luck", part 4 of five contiguous nights; begins “And when he reached the last village, he saw a knife-grinder with his”; ends “over the goose to the pedlar and received the grindstone in exchange.”

questions.prompt: Why does the grinder keep asking where each earlier possession came from?
facilitatorNotes: The questions reconstruct Hans’s whole chain of exchanges. They also let the listener measure the long journey from a large wage to a goose.
evidence: And the gold?

questions.prompt: Which part of the grinder’s description of his trade sounds almost magical to Hans?
facilitatorNotes: Finding money every time a hand goes into a pocket seems effortless and never-ending, although grinding is work. Ask what practical work the promise leaves out.
evidence: every time he puts his hand in his pocket finds money there

questions.prompt: What warning about the grindstone does the grinder include, and how much attention does Hans give it?
facilitatorNotes: The stone is a little damaged, but Hans responds to the dream of constant money rather than questioning its condition. The passage shows eagerness, not an examination of the tool.
evidence: it is a little damaged

days.title: Hans in Luck, part 5: an unexpectedly light journey
days.challenge: Notice that losing possessions produces joy rather than the expected regret.
days.focus: The ending invites different judgments about luck and freedom from burdens.
days.context: Recap: Hans has exchanged his goose for a grindstone, and the grinder has added an ordinary stone. These are the closing paragraphs of the tale.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Hans in Luck", part 5 of five contiguous nights; begins “"Now," said the knife-grinder, taking up a heavy common stone that”; ends “So on he went, void of care, until he reached his mother's house.”

questions.prompt: How does the second stone repeat Hans’s original problem with his gold?
facilitatorNotes: Both are heavy burdens carried on the road. Though their monetary value differs, Hans again wants relief from weight.
evidence: the stones weighed him down most unmercifully

questions.prompt: Does Hans deliberately throw away his stones? Why does that distinction matter to his idea of luck?
facilitatorNotes: No; he accidentally nudges them while drinking. He sees his relief as something fortunate that happens without effort.
evidence: he happened to give the stones a little push

questions.prompt: Would every reader call Hans the luckiest man? Compare two possible views using the ending.
facilitatorNotes: A listener may value his carefree return or regret the wages he has lost. Both can be supported; avoid making one moral compulsory.
evidence: void of care

days.title: The Three Spinsters, part 1: a mother’s boast
days.challenge: Notice how one untrue answer creates the whole problem of the story.
days.focus: A lie told out of shame turns into an impossible task.
days.context: In this Grimm tale, in Lucy Crane’s translation, flax is the plant whose fibres are spun into linen thread on a spinning-wheel.
days.contentNote: The tale opens with a mother beating her daughter for refusing to spin; it is told in one sentence.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "The Three Spinsters", opening through the Queen’s order; begins “THE THREE SPINSTERS”; ends “"To-morrow you must begin to work."”

questions.prompt: Why does the mother tell the Queen the opposite of the truth about her daughter?
facilitatorNotes: She is ashamed of the girl’s laziness, so she claims the girl spins too much. Some children call it a quick trick, others embarrassment; both fit “ashamed.”
evidence: The woman was ashamed to tell of her daughter's laziness

questions.prompt: What does the Queen promise if all the flax is spun, and why does she say being poor does not matter?
facilitatorNotes: Her eldest son as bridegroom; she says the girl’s industry is dowry enough. The promise rests on the mother’s lie, which the listener knows and the Queen does not.
evidence: your industry is dowry enough

questions.prompt: The girl spins nothing for three days. What excuse does she give, and is it the whole truth?
facilitatorNotes: She says she is too sad at leaving her home and mother. The narrator has told us the real reason: she could never spin so much. Her excuse may be partly true as well.
evidence: she could not have spun the flax, even if she were to live to be a hundred years old
because of the distress she was in at leaving her home and her mother

days.title: The Three Spinsters, part 2: help with a condition
days.challenge: Track three separate spinning jobs and the three questions that later explain them.
days.focus: A promise to acknowledge helpers in public changes the young woman’s future.
days.context: Recap: because of her mother’s boast, the lazy girl must spin three rooms of flax at the Queen’s castle, and the Queen has promised her eldest son to her when it is done. She has told the girl to begin tomorrow.
days.contentNote: The bridegroom calls the three women ugly when he sees them; each explains her unusual feature by years of spinning.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "The Three Spinsters", from the girl’s search for help to the end of the tale; begins “When the girl found herself alone again she could not tell how to”; ends “And so she escaped that tiresome flax-spinning.”

questions.prompt: What do the three women ask for besides an invitation to the wedding?
facilitatorNotes: They ask not to be treated with shame, to be called cousins and to sit at the table. The request concerns public respect and belonging.
evidence: not be ashamed of us

questions.prompt: How does the description of spinning show cooperation rather than three people doing the same thing?
facilitatorNotes: One draws thread and works the treadle, another moistens it and the third twists it. Each contributes a different part.
evidence: the second moistened the thread

questions.prompt: What shared explanation do the women give for the features the bridegroom questions?
facilitatorNotes: Their feet, lips and thumbs have been affected by repeated spinning work. The answers turn his attention from appearance to labour.
evidence: With twisting thread

questions.prompt: How does the bridegroom’s final decision change the meaning of the women’s help?
facilitatorNotes: They have not only completed the flax; their testimony frees the bride from future spinning. A child may see a clever plan or an unexpected result.
evidence: should never touch a spinning-wheel

days.title: Antonio Canova, part 1: a chance to try
days.challenge: Carry early clues about a child’s interests into a later problem.
days.focus: A household emergency creates an opening for an overlooked skill.
days.context: Baldwin tells a traditional anecdote about the sculptor’s childhood. “Count” is a noble title, and a sculptor makes figures from materials such as clay or stone.
days.contentNote: The opening mentions that Antonio’s father has died.

excerpt.locator: Antonio Canova, part 1: a chance to try; source blocks 963–982, beginning “A good many years ago there lived in Italy a little boy whose name was An-to´ni-o Ca-no´va” and ending “And so, since nothing else could be done, the man allowed him to try.”.

questions.prompt: How do Antonio’s two grandparents help his imagination in different ways?
facilitatorNotes: His grandfather offers the stone-yard and encourages his making; his grandmother’s stories supply pictures to turn into shapes.
evidence: try to make some of those pictures in stone or clay.

questions.prompt: Why does the broken statue worry the servants so much?
facilitatorNotes: They fear the Count’s anger over an improperly arranged table. Their fear makes the situation feel urgent.
evidence: The Count would be very angry.

questions.prompt: Who gives Antonio a chance when one man laughs at him?
facilitatorNotes: The other servants who know him ask that he be allowed to try. Knowing his work changes how they judge the offer.
evidence: Let the boy try what he can do,

days.title: Antonio Canova, part 2: the butter lion
days.challenge: Separate an impressive first success from the teaching that follows.
days.focus: Unusual material reveals skill that adults had overlooked.
days.context: Antonio has permission to replace a broken dinner-table statue. There is little time before the Count’s guests arrive.

excerpt.locator: Antonio Canova, part 2: the butter lion; source blocks 983–995, beginning “On the kitchen table there was a large square lump of yellow butter. Two hundred pounds th” and ending “d marble. In a few years, Antonio Canova became known as one of the greatest sculptors in the world.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the lion surprise the guests in two different ways?
facilitatorNotes: They admire its skillful form, and then discover it is made from butter rather than a usual sculpting material.
evidence: how odd that he should choose to make it of butter!

questions.prompt: How does Antonio’s position at the dinner change?
facilitatorNotes: He begins working in the kitchen and ends sitting among the honored guests. The attention follows his demonstrated work.
evidence: Antonio should have a seat with them;

questions.prompt: Does one butter lion instantly make him a trained sculptor?
facilitatorNotes: The Count arranges teaching by artists, and the story then passes through several years. Talent is supported by learning and practice.
evidence: The best artists in the land were em-ployed to teach him

days.title: Shepherdess Walk
days.challenge: Picture fanciful sheep, then reconsider whether finding them is the real point of the walk.
days.focus: The ending values companionship as much as a search for marvels.
days.context: A shepherdess tends sheep. A ram, ewe, lamb, and wether are different kinds of sheep; ebony is a dark wood. The poem gives the animals impossible jewel-like features. Read its last question as an invitation.

excerpt.locator: Shepherdess Walk; complete poem, opening “Walk, Shepherdess, walk,”, closing “I shan't mind—shall you?”.

questions.prompt: Which details make these sheep seem imagined rather than ordinary?
facilitatorNotes: Gold feet, silver fleece, an ebony horn, and a crystal bell create a marvellous flock. Any two supported details work.
evidence: the gold-footed ewe;
The lamb with the fleece of silver

questions.prompt: Which animal helps the others find their way, and how?
facilitatorNotes: The wether wears a crystal bell and leads them home. The bell can be imagined as a sound to follow, though the text does not explain all its practical details.
evidence:
And the wether with the crystal bell
That leads them all home.

questions.prompt: What do the last two lines suggest the speaker enjoys even if the search fails?
facilitatorNotes: Walking together may matter more than finding the flock. The speaker says not finding them would not spoil the outing and asks whether the companion agrees.
evidence:
And if we never find them
I shan't mind—shall you?

days.title: Mother Hulda, part 1: down the well
days.challenge: Follow the girl from hardship at home into a magic world, then from one talking object to the next.
days.focus: Ordinary household work is enlarged into an explanation of snow.
days.context: A spindle is the rod on which spun thread is wound. The mark [A] points to the book’s own footnote, which comes at the end of the tale in tomorrow’s reading.
days.contentNote: A stepmother makes her stepdaughter spin until her fingers bleed and scolds her without mercy; in despair the girl jumps into the well and wakes in a magic meadow. The tale calls one daughter pretty and the other ugly, a common pattern in old fairy tales.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Mother Hulda", opening through the girl’s life with Mother Hulda; begins “MOTHER HULDA”; ends “she had a great longing to go home. At last she said to her mistress,”

questions.prompt: Why does the girl jump into the well?
facilitatorNotes: Her stepmother orders her to fetch the spindle back, and she does not know what else to do. The tale moves from hardship into a magic meadow without explaining how.
evidence: you must go and fetch it out again!
in the despair of her heart

questions.prompt: How does the girl know when the bread and apples need help?
facilitatorNotes: Each speaks and names its readiness: baked bread risks burning and ripe apples ask to be shaken. Their voices make ordinary tasks into encounters.
evidence: we apples are all of us ripe!

questions.prompt: Why does the girl change her mind after being frightened by the old woman’s teeth?
facilitatorNotes: The woman speaks kindly, so the girl judges her by how she behaves rather than only by appearance.
evidence: As the old woman spoke so kindly

questions.prompt: What everyday movement becomes magical in Mother Hulda’s explanation?
facilitatorNotes: Shaking a feather bed makes feathers fly, which the story connects with snowfall in the world. Distinguish the tale’s image from a science explanation.
evidence: and then in the world it snows

days.title: Mother Hulda, part 2: gold and pitch
days.challenge: Compare two journeys along the same path, step by step.
days.focus: Matching episodes show two characters choosing differently in the same places.
days.context: Recap: the girl fell into a well, helped the bread and the apples in a magic meadow, and worked kindly for Mother Hulda, shaking her feather bed so that it snowed in the world. The last line, marked [A], is the book’s footnote.
days.contentNote: The lazy sister is punished: a kettle of pitch is emptied over her and never comes off.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "Mother Hulda", from the girl’s homesickness to the end of the tale and its footnote; begins “"I am home-sick, and although I am very well off here, I cannot stay”; ends “In Hesse, when it snows, they say, "Mother Hulda is making her bed."”
excerpt.inlineReason: The night ends with the tale’s footnote in the form “[A] In Hesse, when it snows…”; the library work grimm-household-stories-crane-1886 now sets each printed note as its own block “[Footnote A: …]” (the library’s note convention), so the night is not a range of it. The story text and the note’s words agree.

blocks.text: "I am home-sick, and although I am very well off here, I cannot stay any longer; I must go back to my own home."
Mother Hulda answered,
"It pleases me well that you should wish to go home, and, as you have served me faithfully, I will undertake to send you there!"

She took her by the hand and led her to a large door standing open, and as she was passing through it there fell upon her a heavy shower of gold, and the gold hung all about her, so that she was covered with it.

"All this is yours, because you have been so industrious," said Mother Hulda; and, besides that, she returned to her her spindle, the very same that she had dropped in the well. And then the door was shut again, and the girl found herself back again in the world, not far from her mother's house; and as she passed through the yard the cock stood on the top of the well and cried,

"Cock-a-doodle doo!
Our golden girl has come home too!"
Then she went in to her mother, and as she had returned covered with gold she was well received.

So the girl related all her history, and what had happened to her, and when the mother heard how she came to have such great riches she began to wish that her ugly and idle daughter might have the same good fortune. So she sent her to sit by the well and spin; and in order to make her spindle bloody she put her hand into the thorn hedge. Then she threw the spindle into the well, and jumped in herself. She found herself, like her sister, in the beautiful meadow, and followed the same path, and when she came to the baker's oven, the bread cried out,
"Oh, take me out, take me out, or I shall burn; I am quite done already!"
But the lazy-bones answered,
"I have no desire to black my hands," and went on farther. Soon she came to the apple-tree, who called out,
"Oh, shake me, shake me, we apples are all of us ripe!"
But she answered,

"That is all very fine; suppose one of you should fall on my head," and went on farther. When she came to Mother Hulda's house she did not feel afraid, as she knew beforehand of her great teeth, and entered into her service at once. The first day she put her hand well to the work, and was industrious, and did everything Mother Hulda bade her, because of the gold she expected; but the second day she began to be idle, and the third day still more so, so that she would not get up in the morning. Neither did she make Mother Hulda's bed as it ought to have been made, and did not shake it for the feathers to fly about. So that Mother Hulda soon grew tired of her, and gave her warning, at which the lazy thing was well pleased, and thought that now the shower of gold was coming; so Mother Hulda led her to the door, and as she stood in the doorway, instead of the shower of gold a great kettle full of pitch was emptied over her.
"That is the reward for your service," said Mother Hulda, and shut the door. So the lazy girl came home all covered with pitch, and the cock on the top of the well seeing her, cried,

"Cock-a-doodle doo!
Our dirty girl has come home too!"
And the pitch remained sticking to her fast, and never, as long as she lived, could it be got off.
[A] In Hesse, when it snows, they say, "Mother Hulda is making her bed."

questions.prompt: Does the girl say she has been unhappy with Mother Hulda? What makes her request more complicated?
facilitatorNotes: She says she is very well off, yet cannot stay because she longs for home. Both feelings coexist.
evidence: although I am very well off here

questions.prompt: How does Mother Hulda’s answer differ from forbidding the girl to leave?
facilitatorNotes: She is pleased by the wish and offers to send her home. Her kindness includes helping her leave.
evidence: I will undertake to send you there!

questions.prompt: Why is returning the spindle more personal than simply giving gold?
facilitatorNotes: It is the very object the girl lost and connects her adventure to where she began. Gold rewards work, while the spindle restores something particular.
evidence: the very same that she had dropped in the well

questions.prompt: The second daughter follows the same path. Name two places where she acts differently from her sister, and say what each girl brings home.
facilitatorNotes: She refuses the bread and the apples, and works hard for one day only before growing idle; she comes home covered in pitch instead of gold. The cock’s two rhymes mark the match. Some children find the ending fair, others harsh; the tale says only that the pitch never came off.
evidence: I have no desire to black my hands
Our dirty girl has come home too!

days.title: The Two Wishes
days.challenge: Track how testing a gift uses up the gift itself.
days.focus: A careless experiment requires its own reversal.
days.context: Here “faggot-maker” means a person who bundles firewood; it is an old occupational term. An angel offers two wishes for food and drink.
days.contentNote: The trapped man feels pain before escaping unharmed. The angel and wishes belong to a fairy-tale religious setting; the drink is unspecified.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “YE TWO WISHES”, beginning “An Angel went a walking out one day, as I've heard said,
And, coming t”, ending “or wisdom, which, when we had in store,
I'm very doubtful if we'd care to ask for anymore.”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 88.

questions.prompt: Why does the man wish to enter the bottle?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to test whether the offer is true, not because being inside is useful.
evidence: just as a test,

questions.prompt: What must he spend his second wish on?
facilitatorNotes: He must undo the first wish and escape. He ends with no lasting benefit from either.
evidence: he had to wish once more.

questions.prompt: Why might wisdom be a useful first wish in the final verse?
facilitatorNotes: It could help him judge what is worth wanting and avoid the wasteful experiment. Children can question whether wisdom would remove every other wish.
evidence: For first we'd ask for wisdom,

days.title: The Brownies Tobogganing — Making their own sleds (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow an alternative plan from suggestion to completed work.
days.focus: Different kinds of skill combine to make a new winter pleasure possible.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. A toboggan is a long sled. The opening ends when the Brownies finish making theirs; the later ride is outside this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES TOBOGGANING Text blocks 1–6; opening “ONE evening, when the snow lay white”; closing “Soon brought their labors to an end.”.

questions.prompt: How does the second plan change the first idea for getting toboggans?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of finding finished sleds in a shop, they will build them from lumber.
evidence: And make toboggans of our own;

questions.prompt: What makes bringing the wood back difficult even before construction begins?
facilitatorNotes: Heavy boards and wind tax both their strength and patience.
evidence: It chanced to be a windy night,

questions.prompt: Which three advantages help the work finish quickly, and which does the narrator call better still?
facilitatorNotes: There are many workers, they have skill, and they are willing. The narrator especially values willing hands; connect that phrase to the effort already shown.
evidence: And hands were willing--better still;

days.title: The Brownies' Balloon — An unexpected anchor (excerpt)
days.challenge: Remember an object’s earlier use when it gains a new use near the end.
days.focus: A comic accident becomes the means of escape.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have repaired and filled an abandoned balloon with gas. This excerpt begins when it pulls free, taking a stump and garden gate along. Its impossible flight is fantasy.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES' BALLOON. Text blocks 6–11; opening “But strong it grew and stronger still,”; closing “From placing scare-crows in their grain.”.

questions.prompt: What do the stump and gate first provide for Brownies who lack seats?
facilitatorNotes: They become improvised supports. Later the stump has a second role, so ask children to keep it in mind.
evidence: And furnished seats they highly prized.

questions.prompt: Why do the passengers change from wanting to rise to wanting to descend?
facilitatorNotes: The moon still looks far away, and the familiar earth with its grass, shade and birds begins to seem better.
evidence: The moon looks just as far away.

questions.prompt: How does something they never meant to take help them land?
facilitatorNotes: The stump catches in branches and acts as an anchor, holding the balloon. Its accidental presence becomes useful.
evidence: And, as an anchor, played a part

days.title: The Golden Goose, part 1: two brothers in the forest
days.challenge: Compare two similar episodes and predict the third.
days.focus: Repetition sets up a pattern that the youngest son will break.
days.context: In this Grimm tale, in Lucy Crane’s translation, the youngest of three sons is mocked with the nickname “the Simpleton.”
days.contentNote: Each older brother refuses to share and then cuts himself with his own hatchet; each injury is told in a sentence.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "The Golden Goose", opening through the father’s permission; begins “THE GOLDEN GOOSE”; ends “"Well, be off with you; you will only learn by experience."”

questions.prompt: What does the little grey man ask each older brother, and how do their answers differ in words but not in meaning?
facilitatorNotes: He asks for cake and wine. The first pretends to have none; the second says plainly that what he gives he loses. Both refuse.
evidence: I haven't got any; be off with you.
What I give you I lose myself

questions.prompt: The narrator says, “That was what came of the little grey man.” What connection does the narrator want us to make?
facilitatorNotes: The accident follows the refusal, and the next brother’s injury is called “the punishment.” The grey man is never shown doing anything, so children may say magic, punishment, or bad luck; ask which words support each.
evidence: That was what came of the little grey man.
The punishment followed

questions.prompt: Why does the father refuse the youngest son at first, and what does he say when he finally gives in?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks the boy “understands nothing” and fears another injury; worn down by begging, he says the boy will only learn by experience. Invite predictions about what the youngest son will learn.
evidence: you understand nothing about it
you will only learn by experience

days.title: The Golden Goose, part 2: a shared meal and a stuck procession
days.challenge: Compare the boy’s modest description of his food with the meal’s magical change.
days.focus: Willingness to share is shown before any reward is promised.
days.context: Recap: both older brothers refused to share their cake and wine with a little grey man and then hurt themselves cutting wood. Now the youngest son sets out with a plain cake and sour beer.

excerpt.locator: Household Stories (Lucy Crane, tr.; Macmillan 1886 text, PG 19068), "The Golden Goose", from the youngest son’s meal through the procession of seven; begins “The mother gave him a cake (it was only made with water, and baked in”; ends “too; and now there were seven following the Simpleton and the goose.”

questions.prompt: What makes the boy’s offer generous even though his food is not grand?
facilitatorNotes: He offers company and a share of what little he has without pretending it is fine food.
evidence: if that is good enough for you, let us sit down together and eat

questions.prompt: When does the old man promise good luck—before or after the boy agrees to share?
facilitatorNotes: After the meal and the willing offer. The sequence matters because the boy does not begin by bargaining for a reward.
evidence: As you have such a kind heart

questions.prompt: How does the innkeeper’s eldest daughter treat the goose differently from the boy’s treatment of his food?
facilitatorNotes: She plans to take a feather for herself rather than ask or share; the contrast helps set up the comic trouble.
evidence: I will pull out one of its feathers for myself

questions.prompt: How does the repeated touching make the final number seven believable rather than random?
facilitatorNotes: Three girls, the parson, the sexton and two peasants join in order. Reconstruct the chain with fingers or named cards.
evidence: now there were seven following the Simpleton and the goose

days.title: The Golden Goose, part 3: three further demands
days.challenge: Remember repeated obstacles after a character appears to have fulfilled the original task.
days.focus: Moving promises and returning kindness shape the ending.
days.context: A golden goose has drawn seven people into a comical stuck-together procession. The youngest son brings it before a princess whom nobody has been able to make laugh.
days.contentNote: The thirsty man’s drinking is exaggerated for comedy. The princess is the king’s promised reward, a convention of old fairy tales.

excerpt.locator: The Golden Goose — three further demands (ending excerpt); source blocks 2550–2563; begins “By and by they came to a town where a king reigned, who had an only daughter who was so se”; ends “the death of the king the Simpleton possessed the kingdom, and lived long and happily with his wife.”.

questions.prompt: After the princess laughs, does her father immediately keep his advertised promise?
facilitatorNotes: No. He sets new conditions because he dislikes the young man as a son-in-law. Ask the listener to distinguish the original challenge from later demands.
evidence: made all kinds of objections

questions.prompt: Why are the extremely thirsty and hungry men useful here instead of merely troublesome?
facilitatorNotes: Their unusual needs exactly match the king’s impossible demands. A difficulty becomes an ability in the right situation.
evidence: eat up a mountain of bread

questions.prompt: What final explanation connects the old man’s help to the meal shared earlier?
facilitatorNotes: He says he supplied the eating, drinking and ship because the boy was kind first. The ending explicitly returns to the first encounter.
evidence: all because you were kind to me at the first

days.title: The Bell of Atri, part 1: a bell anyone can reach
days.challenge: See how a physical detail supports or defeats a fair rule.
days.focus: The bell’s rope makes a public promise of justice accessible.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words. This first scene explains the bell and the repair that prepares the next scene.

excerpt.locator: The Bell of Atri, part 1: a bell anyone can reach; source blocks 407–422, beginning “A-tri is the name of a little town in It-a-ly. It is a very old town, and is built half-wa” and ending “"Yes," said the judges, "it is a very good rope. Let it be as it is."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the king leave the new bell silent at the celebration?
facilitatorNotes: It is reserved for a person who has been wronged, not a ceremonial performance.
evidence: it must never be rung except in case of need.

questions.prompt: What changes when the rope wears short?
facilitatorNotes: Only tall people can reach it, so the original promise no longer works for everyone.
evidence: only a tall man could reach it.

questions.prompt: Why do the judges accept a grapevine instead of waiting for a proper rope?
facilitatorNotes: Someone might need justice during the delay. The vine restores access immediately, although its leaves will have an unexpected effect later.
evidence: What if some great wrong should be done before it came?

days.title: The Bell of Atri, part 2: the hungry horse
days.challenge: Distinguish an accidental signal from the real need it reveals.
days.focus: An animal’s hunger brings a human failure into public view.
days.context: The town’s bell calls judges to hear a wrong. Its worn rope has just been replaced with a leafy grapevine.
days.contentNote: An old horse is starved, abandoned, and has stones thrown at it. The story condemns the neglect and ends with food and shelter. “Dumb” here means unable to speak.

excerpt.locator: The Bell of Atri, part 2: the hungry horse; source blocks 423–438, beginning “Now, on the hill-side above the village, there lived a man who had once been a brave knigh” and ending “ joy, and the horse was led away to his new stall and a dinner such as he had not had in many a day.”.

questions.prompt: Does the horse pull the vine in order to ask the judges for help?
facilitatorNotes: It wants food. The accidental ringing nevertheless brings attention to a genuine wrong.
evidence: What a fine dinner they would be for a starving horse!

questions.prompt: How do the judges learn what the owner has done?
facilitatorNotes: The town knows the horse’s condition, and people tell how they have seen it wandering neglected. The decision draws on that history, not only a ringing bell.
evidence: every one was ready to tell how they had seen him

questions.prompt: How does the judgment connect the horse’s earlier work to its future care?
facilitatorNotes: Because the horse helped the knight gain wealth and survive danger, part of that wealth must provide shelter and food now.
evidence: He has helped you gain your wealth.

days.title: The Elves — the maid’s visit (complete second story)
days.challenge: Notice the difference between time as the maid experiences it and time outside the mountain.
days.focus: An unchanged object makes a magical time-shift more surprising.
days.context: This is the second independent story in Grimm’s group titled The Elves. It is not the shoemaker story. A servant receives an unexpected invitation.
days.contentNote: The final sentence says that the maid’s former employers have died during her long absence; there is no death scene. Explain that magical time is part of the tale.

excerpt.locator: The Elves — the maid’s visit (complete second story); source blocks 1685–1686; begins “(II.)”; ends “en years with the elves in the mountain, and that during that time her master and mistress had died.”.

questions.prompt: How does the maid find out what the letter says, and why does that detail matter?
facilitatorNotes: She asks her employers to read it because she cannot read. It shows her practical solution and helps introduce the invitation without pretending everyone then had reading opportunities.
evidence: as she could not read

questions.prompt: Which details make the small mountain household seem splendid rather than poor?
facilitatorNotes: The pearl-studded ebony bed, golden embroidery, ivory cradle and gold bath suggest richness on a tiny scale. Accept any precise pair.
evidence: a bed made of ebony, studded with pearls

questions.prompt: Why does finding the broom where she left it make the ending especially strange?
facilitatorNotes: It looks as if she can simply resume work, but strangers reveal seven years have passed. The familiar broom contrasts with the changed people.
evidence: it was still standing in the corner where she had left it

days.title: How They Bring Back the Village of Cream Puffs When the Wind Blows It Away
days.workTitle: How They Bring Back the Village of Cream Puffs When the Wind Blows It Away
days.challenge: Follow a story told inside a story, and notice descriptions that are repeated almost word for word.
days.focus: Repetition and an invented machine make an impossible floating village sound orderly and believable.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. Wing Tip the Spick is visiting four uncles in the Village of Liver-and-Onions and tells them about her own home.
days.contentNote: “Wing Tip the Spick” is one of Sandburg’s invented nonsense names. The same sound, usually spelled “spic,” is an offensive American slur for Spanish-speaking people; nothing in the story connects the name with that meaning.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), part 1, "How They Bring Back the Village of Cream Puffs When the Wind Blows It Away", beginning p. 19; complete story, from "A girl named Wing Tip the Spick came to the Village of Liver-and-Onions" to "I am going to have a sweet time visiting my relations."

questions.prompt: The uncles on her mother’s side and the uncles on her father’s side each describe Wing Tip’s blue eyes. What do you notice when you compare the two descriptions?
facilitatorNotes: The two speeches are nearly identical; the second adds “shining” and “the.” Some children think the uncles copy each other; others hear both sides of the family loving her equally. Either reading fits. The uncles repeat the description a third time at the end, so the repetition works like a song refrain.
evidence: such a clear light blue, they are the same as cornflowers
such a clear light shining blue, they are the same as cornflowers

questions.prompt: How do the people of Cream Puffs bring their village back after the rough wind blows it into the sky? Tell the steps in order.
facilitatorNotes: A long string on a big spool in the roundhouse is fastened to the village; it unwinds as the wind carries the village off; when the wind has had its fun, everyone winds the spool together. Children may compare it to flying a kite. Ask why the whole village must help.
evidence: you will see a big spool with a long string winding up around the spool
the people of the village all come together and begin to wind up the spool

questions.prompt: Wing Tip says her mother put the two freckles on her chin. What job do the freckles do, and why might a mother want that?
facilitatorNotes: They remind her each morning where she came from and that she must not stay away too long. Some children hear love or homesickness; others hear a funny village rule. The freckles look like “little burnt cream puffs,” tying them to the village’s name.
evidence: They remind her where she came from and she mustn’t stay away too long.

days.title: Never Kick a Slipper at the Moon
days.workTitle: Never Kick a Slipper at the Moon
days.challenge: Hear how a rule is explained by a story, and notice how the ending returns to the opening advice.
days.focus: A father’s warning grows into a small myth; a list of different ways of walking makes a night parade of empty shoes vivid.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. Mr. Wishes is giving advice to his daughter, Peter Potato Blossom Wishes, a girl who appears in several Rootabaga stories. A “Dancing Slipper Moon” is his name for a thin new moon.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), "Never Kick a Slipper at the Moon", beginning p. 185; complete story, from "When a girl is growing up in the Rootabaga Country" to "like the toe and the heel of a dancer’s foot." The following numbered section heading is excluded.

questions.prompt: What does the Dancing Slipper Moon look like, according to Mr. Wishes?
facilitatorNotes: The slim early moon looks like the toe and the heel of a dancer’s foot. Children can draw the shape or curve a hand to show it; the picture explains why a slipper might fit the moon.
evidence: the slim early moon looks like the toe and the heel of a dancer’s foot

questions.prompt: When the shoes go walking without feet, they walk in many different ways. Choose one way you could act out. Which words tell you how to do it?
facilitatorNotes: Possible choices include pussyfoot, clumping, pigeon-toe, running glad and fast, or lagging slow and sorry. The repeated “just like people in the daytime” suggests the shoes copy the people who wear them.
evidence: Some walked pussyfoot, sliding easy and soft just like people in the daytime.
some lagged slow and sorry

questions.prompt: Is the story of the girl’s lost slipper a good reason for the rule? Why do you think fathers and mothers in the Rootabaga Country keep telling it?
facilitatorNotes: Some children accept the evidence: the slipper never came back. Others notice that nobody saw it reach the moon and think parents tell it because it is a good story or a way to say “take care of your things.” Both views can be supported; the story calls itself “the explanations” and leaves the judgment to the listener.
evidence: It never came back, that slipper. It was never seen again.
And these are the explanations why fathers and mothers in the Rootabaga Country

days.title: The Wedding Procession of the Rag Doll and the Broom Handle and Who Was in It
days.workTitle: The Wedding Procession of the Rag Doll and the Broom Handle and Who Was in It
days.challenge: Keep a long list of marchers in order and notice the sentence pattern that ends each group’s description.
days.focus: A catalogue structure, invented group names and a repeated refrain turn kitchen mess into a parade.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. In this story household things such as a rag doll, a broom handle and a coffee pot act like people, and each group of marchers is named for what it does.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), part 4, "The Wedding Procession of the Rag Doll and the Broom Handle and Who Was in It", beginning p. 99; complete story, from "The Rag Doll had many friends." to "It was a grand procession, don’t you think so?"

questions.prompt: Why did the Rag Doll choose the Broom Handle to marry?
facilitatorNotes: He fixed her eyes with two black California prunes after a careless child knocked off her glass eyes. Children may call it gratitude, kindness or simply that he helped when it mattered; each answer should point to the prunes.
evidence: it was the Broom Handle she picked because the Broom Handle fixed her eyes

questions.prompt: Almost every group’s description ends the same way: the marchers do something, look around, and do it again. Which group breaks that pattern at the very end, and why does the change fit them?
facilitatorNotes: The Sleepyheads “never looked around at all” because they are almost asleep. Breaking the pattern signals the end of the procession, like the end of a long day. Some children also notice the Sleepyheads are smiling and glad even though they are fading.
evidence: they licked their spoons and looked around and licked their spoons again
the Sleepyheads they never looked around at all

questions.prompt: About the Clean Ears the story says, “How they got into the procession nobody knows.” Why might they seem out of place?
facilitatorNotes: The other groups are sticky, noisy, messy or silly; the Clean Ears are proud and spotless. Children may hear a joke about grown-up rules for washing. Accept other reasons tied to particular details of the other groups.
evidence: How they got into the procession nobody knows.
There was not a speck of dirt or dust or muss or mess

questions.prompt: Which made-up word in the description of the Musical Soup Eaters sounds most like what it describes? Say it aloud.
facilitatorNotes: “Chuzzled” and “snozzled” both imitate slurping. Let children argue for one by how it feels to say it; the invented words belong to the same play with sound as “Chubby Chubs” and “slimpsing.”
evidence: They whistled and chuzzled and snozzled the soup

days.title: Superficial Culture
days.challenge: Distinguish a learned performance from a creature’s underlying nature.
days.focus: Elaborate manners cannot turn the comic pig into a human speaker.
days.context: “Deportment” means manners and bearing; “gentility” means the social polish valued by the characters.
days.contentNote: The poem satirizes social rank through a talking pig. Its comparison should not be used to rank real people’s worth by background or speech.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “SUPERFICIAL CULTURE”, beginning “I'll tell of a certain old dame;
        The same
Had a beautiful pigg”, ending “or, whatever his polish might be,
        Why, dear me!
He was pig at the bottom, you see.”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 46.

questions.prompt: What does the dancing master successfully teach James?
facilitatorNotes: His manners in company become polished and hard to criticize. The teaching does work within that particular task.
evidence: So his company manners were rare.

questions.prompt: What one sound interrupts all the elegant description?
facilitatorNotes: The pig squeals when he tries to speak. Say the sound after the long formal words to hear the comic contrast.
evidence: O w-e-e-k!

questions.prompt: Does being a pig mean James did nothing well?
facilitatorNotes: No: the earlier verses explicitly praise his manners. The ending limits what outward polish can change; it need not erase everything he learned.
evidence: whatever his polish might be,

days.title: The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy, part 1: two neighbors go away
days.workTitle: The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy
days.challenge: Compare two characters described in matching patterns, then read a short letter for clues.
days.focus: Parallel description—three white horses, three blue winds—prepares a mystery about where two friends have gone.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. This is a story that parents in the Rootabaga Country tell their children in the evening. Listen for how the girl and the boy are described in the same pattern.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), part 6, "The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy", beginning p. 159; opening excerpt, from "When the dishes are washed at night time" through the letter and "to guess and guess where two darlings had gone." Continues next night.

questions.prompt: The White Horse Girl has three white horses and the Blue Wind Boy has three blue winds. What are the three of each?
facilitatorNotes: Horses white as snow, as new washed sheep wool, and as silver; winds of the daytime, of the night, and of the times between night and day. Children can line them up in two columns to see how the story matches them.
evidence: She rode one horse white as snow, another horse white as new washed sheep wool, and another white as silver.
a blue wind of the times between night and day

questions.prompt: The Boy says each wind does something different for him. Which wind would you most like to listen to, and what does he say it does?
facilitatorNotes: The morning wind believes and remembers what he tells it; the night wind understands his secrets; the dusk wind asks questions and tells him to wait. Any choice works if the child names what that wind does.
evidence: the night wind gets inside of me and understands all my secrets
this is the wind that asks me questions and tells me to wait

questions.prompt: Read the letter they left once more. What clues does it give about where they went, and what does it leave out?
facilitatorNotes: It joins their two loves—where white horses come from and where blue winds begin—but names no place and gives no reason, so the families must guess. Invite predictions (the sea, the sky, the far west) and keep them for the next night.
evidence: We have started to go where the white horses come from and where the blue winds begin.
Nobody at all knew beforehand or afterward why they were going away

days.title: The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy, part 2: the Gray Man’s report
days.workTitle: The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy
days.challenge: Use the earlier descriptions to solve a picture puzzle in a traveler’s report.
days.focus: Metaphor: sea waves become white horses, and the line where sea meets sky becomes the place where winds begin.
days.context: Recap: the White Horse Girl loved her three white horses and the Blue Wind Boy loved three blue winds. One day both went away, leaving a short letter saying they had gone where the white horses come from and where the blue winds begin.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), "The White Horse Girl and the Blue Wind Boy", closing excerpt, from "Many years passed. One day there came riding across the Rootabaga Country a Gray Man on Horseback." to the end of the story, "the lamps and fires are lit for the night in winter."

questions.prompt: What does the Gray Man on Horseback see when he finds the two of them?
facilitatorNotes: They sit together among high, tough rocks, looking across blue water that meets the blue sky; white horses come toward land by thousands and millions. Encourage children to name several details in order.
evidence: blue water as far as the eye could see

questions.prompt: The white horses coming toward the land have “white manes, white flanks, white noses, white galloping feet.” What real thing at the seashore could they be?
facilitatorNotes: Many children will think of waves with white foam or whitecaps, especially near where “the blue waters met the blue sky.” Others prefer real magic horses; the story allows both. Point out that the same body parts were used for the Girl’s ponies in part 1, so the story is turning the sea into her horses.
evidence: there were white manes, white flanks, white noses, white galloping feet
some white as snow, some like new washed sheep wool, some white as silver ribbons of the new moon

questions.prompt: The families wonder whether the Gray Man made up his story. What do you think, and which details help you decide?
facilitatorNotes: The story never settles it. A child may trust him because his report fits the letter, or doubt him because he “would tell” no more and nobody can check. Ask for one detail on each side.
