evidence: whether the Gray Man on Horseback made up the story out of his head or whether it happened just like he told it

questions.prompt: Last night’s part began, “When the dishes are washed at night time.” Tonight’s ending uses almost the same words. Why might a storyteller end where the story began?
facilitatorNotes: It frames the tale as something families tell again and again, and it brings listeners home after the faraway journey. Some children say it makes the story feel finished or sleepy, like a bedtime story.
evidence: when the dishes are washed at night and the cool of the evening has come in summer

days.title: How Gimme the Ax Found Out About the Zigzag Railroad and Who Made It Zigzag
days.workTitle: How Gimme the Ax Found Out About the Zigzag Railroad and Who Made It Zigzag
days.challenge: Follow a tall-tale explanation and notice the same sentence spoken by two opposing groups.
days.focus: A “why” story invents a cause, the zizzies, and builds a back-and-forth contest that the zigzag side wins.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. Gimme the Ax is a father in the Rootabaga Country. The Potato Face Blind Man, who plays an accordion near the post office, tells several of the book’s tales.
days.contentNote: The storyteller’s nickname, the Potato Face Blind Man, describes his face and his blindness. In the book he is a respected, inventive storyteller who appears in several stories.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), part 2, "How Gimme the Ax Found Out About the Zigzag Railroad and Who Made It Zigzag", beginning p. 65; complete story, from "One day Gimme the Ax said to himself" to "it was the same kind of zigzag each had together." The following numbered section heading is excluded.

questions.prompt: Gimme the Ax goes downtown hoping to hear about something that happened while he slept. What silly happenings does he imagine?
facilitatorNotes: A policeman who laughed, fell in a cistern and came out with goldfish wearing jewelry; the man in the moon breaking a pitcher of buttermilk on the cellar stairs. His wild guesses prepare listeners for an even wilder explanation.
evidence: Maybe a policeman began laughing and fell in a cistern and came out with a wheelbarrow full of goldfish wearing new jewelry.

questions.prompt: Describe a zizzy. Which words in the description sound zigzag themselves?
facilitatorNotes: A bug that runs, eats and spits zigzag. The repeated z sounds, and “hizzing with little hizzers,” make the words buzz and twist. Let children say the sentence quickly.
evidence: He runs zigzag on zigzag legs, eats zigzag with zigzag teeth, and spits zigzag with a zigzag tongue.

questions.prompt: Both the workmen and the zizzies say, “This is it—we done it.” What does it show that the two sides say exactly the same words?
facilitatorNotes: Each side is proud of its work and neither is a villain; the contest could go on forever, though the zizzies have the last turn, so the tracks stay zigzag. The workmen’s “we done it” is everyday spoken English, kept as Sandburg wrote it.
evidence: This is it—we done it.

questions.prompt: Who told the Potato Face Blind Man the story? Does that make it more believable or less?
facilitatorNotes: Two little zizzies told it after sleeping in his warm accordion. Some children say they should know, since they did it; others laugh that the troublemakers are the only witnesses and that they “told it zigzag.”
evidence: Two little zizzies.
Both told it zigzag

days.title: A voice at the fireplace (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use overheard conversation to identify a visitor before he is fully seen.
days.focus: A practical chimney problem opens into a secret Christmas encounter.
days.context: Jimmieboy is waiting for Christmas. A velocipede is an early kind of pedal cycle; he calls it a philocipede. This opening ends when he recognizes his visitor.

excerpt.locator: I. Christmas Eve at Jimmieboy’s; opening “It had been a long and trying day to Jimmieboy, as December 24th usually is to childr”; closing “o have him see him or not, so he closed his eyes as tightly as he could, and pretended to be asleep.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Jimmieboy upset even though he believes he has been especially good?
facilitatorNotes: He expects a pedal cycle as a reward but hears that the chimney is too small. The obstacle is a physical size problem, not a report that he has behaved badly.
evidence: Just because those chimneys are small, I can't have a philocipede

questions.prompt: Why does the suggestion of using the front door not solve the visitors’ problem?
facilitatorNotes: One visitor objects that delivering that way would not be proper for his role. A practical solution runs into the story’s Santa tradition.
evidence: It wouldn't be the proper thing.

questions.prompt: Why does Jimmieboy close his eyes after he sees someone he is delighted to recognize?
facilitatorNotes: He is uncertain whether Santa wants to be seen, so pretends to sleep to protect the secret encounter.
evidence: he didn't know whether Santa Claus would like to have him see him or not

days.title: A very wide-awake listener (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice words used literally and playfully during a bedtime-story negotiation.
days.focus: A sleepy adult accidentally enlarges the story he must tell.
days.context: This is the frame around a fairy tale: Jimmieboy wants a story before dawn. The excerpt stops as father agrees to include both requested characters, before the fairy tale’s events.

excerpt.locator: II. The Dwarf and the Dude Giant; opening “The day had not yet dawned, but Jimmieboy was awake—wide awake. So wide awake was he,”; closing “"And a Dwarf, too," put in Jimmieboy, who did not intend to be cheated out of a half of the story.”.

questions.prompt: Does being “wide awake” really mean Jimmieboy’s wakefulness needs a bed twelve feet wider? What is the narrator doing?
facilitatorNotes: No: the narrator turns an ordinary expression into an impossible size. The exaggeration makes his energy and his father’s discomfort comic.
evidence: not broad enough by some ten or twelve feet to accommodate the breadth of his wakefulness

questions.prompt: What tells us the father’s snore is meant to persuade Jimmieboy rather than being genuine sleep?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explicitly calls it an imitation and explains its purpose. Jimmieboy persists despite the performance.
evidence: not a real one, but one of those imitation snores

questions.prompt: How does offering a choice give the father more work?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmieboy asks for both a Giant and a Dwarf and then reminds him not to omit either. The attempted choice becomes a doubled request.
evidence: "Both," said Jimmieboy, placidly.

days.title: How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On, part 1: a cold walk and a new guitar
days.workTitle: How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On
days.challenge: Notice personification—a wind with clamps, mittens as chums—and keep track of a character’s goal.
days.focus: Comparisons and invented sound words make a bitter January walk funny and warm.
days.context: Carl Sandburg wrote these stories for his own young daughters and set them in the Rootabaga Country, an invented prairie land of odd names and villages. Henry Hagglyhoagly is walking on a freezing January night to the house of Susan Slackentwist, the daughter of the rutabaga king. He talks in country speech (“It ain’t,” “I seen”), which Sandburg wrote as people spoke.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), "How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On", beginning p. 175; opening excerpt, from "Sometimes in January the sky comes down close" to "to sing a serenade song.”" Continues next night.

questions.prompt: What do the stars look like to Henry on this January night?
facilitatorNotes: Like the arithmetic writing of a girl just beginning school, with the numbers 4 and 7 written over and over. Children might draw the sky or say which numbers they would see.
evidence: writing number 4 and number 7 and 4 and 7 over and over again across the sky

questions.prompt: How does the wind act like a person or a creature in this part? Which words show it?
facilitatorNotes: It puts “chilly, icy, clammy clamps” on his nose like a nipping clothes pin until the mittens rub it away. Some children see a pinching animal, others a bully; both fit the words.
evidence: put its chilly, icy, clammy clamps on the nose of Henry Hagglyhoagly

questions.prompt: Henry talks to his mittens as if they were kittens, pups or ponies. Why might someone walking alone on a cold night talk to his mittens?
facilitatorNotes: He may be lonely, grateful for warmth, or nervous about the serenade ahead. Others think he is simply a funny, cheerful person. Ask which detail supports each idea.
evidence: You’re my chums keeping me company

questions.prompt: Why did Henry buy a guitar instead of the piano other people suggested? Do you agree with his choice?
facilitatorNotes: The others valued a piano because everyone in the house could play it and because things could be set on top of it—a comic reason. Henry wants something he can carry to Susan’s window. Children may defend either instrument.
evidence: a piano is handy to put a hat and overcoat on or books or flowers

days.title: How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On, part 2: a serenade in the cold
days.workTitle: How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On
days.challenge: Explain how a problem is solved and how one odd act becomes a custom.
days.focus: A practical solution becomes a love test; the ending returns to the opening image of the night sky.
days.context: Recap: on a bitter January night Henry Hagglyhoagly is walking to sing a serenade under Susan Slackentwist’s window. He carries the eight-and-a-half-dollar guitar he bought and talks to his warm wool mittens as if they were friends.

excerpt.locator: Rootabaga Stories (1922), "How Henry Hagglyhoagly Played the Guitar with His Mittens On", closing excerpt, from "The cold wind of the bitter cold weather blew and blew" to the end of the story, "4 and 7 over and over."

questions.prompt: How does Henry know he is near Susan’s house before he gets there?
facilitatorNotes: He stops, lifts his nose and sniffs: he can smell the big rutabaga field near the rutabaga king’s home. His nose, earlier pinched by the wind, now finds the way.
evidence: he stopped, held his nose in the air, and sniffed
this is the big rutabaga field

questions.prompt: What problem does Henry face under the window, and how does he solve it?
facilitatorNotes: If he takes his mittens off, his fingers will freeze too stiff to play, so he plays with them on. Some children wonder how it sounded; the story does not say, but Susan answers with a keepsake.
evidence: I will play with mittens on.

questions.prompt: After that night, what do sweethearts in the Rootabaga Country ask of the people who want to marry them? Why might one odd choice become a custom?
facilitatorNotes: They ask to hear the guitar played under the window on a winter night with wool mittens on. It shows patience and devotion in the cold. Compare the way “Never Kick a Slipper at the Moon” turns one event into a rule.
evidence: let me hear you under my window on a winter night playing the guitar with wool yarn mittens on

questions.prompt: Last night’s part opened with stars that looked like the arithmetic writing of a schoolgirl. Tonight Henry sees the same sky on his way home. What has changed for him, even though the sky looks the same?
facilitatorNotes: He has played his serenade and received a snow-bird feather, and now he expects the guitar to bring luck. Children may say he is happier, warmer inside, or more confident.
evidence: This Spanish Spinnish Splishy guitar made special will bring us luck.

days.title: Oz, chapter II, part 1: the Munchkins and the Witch of the North
days.challenge: Picture a new country through contrast with Kansas, and follow a conversation full of surprises.
days.focus: Dorothy learns the rules of a strange land by asking questions.
days.context: Recap: a cyclone lifted Dorothy’s farmhouse into the sky with Dorothy and her dog Toto inside; after hours of floating, Dorothy fell asleep. Chapter II is “The Council with The Munchkins.”
days.contentNote: The falling house has killed the Wicked Witch of the East; Dorothy sees the witch’s feet in silver shoes sticking out from under it.

excerpt.locator: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (George M. Hill, 1900; PG 43936), chapter II, “The Council with The Munchkins,” first part, to the Witch of the North’s account of the four witches; begins “She was awakened by a shock, so sudden and severe that if Dorothy had”; ends “wicked Witch in all the Land of Oz—the one who lives in the West."”

questions.prompt: How is the land where the house comes down different from the Kansas of chapter I?
facilitatorNotes: Green grass, fruit trees, flowers, bright birds and a sparkling brook, against the “dry, gray prairies” Dorothy knew. The brook’s sound is “very grateful” to a girl from a dry land.
evidence: a little girl who had lived so long on the dry, gray prairies

questions.prompt: Why is Dorothy puzzled when the little woman thanks her for killing the Witch of the East?
facilitatorNotes: Dorothy has never killed anything; her house fell by accident. The Witch says the house did it, “and that is the same thing.” Children may argue about whether Dorothy is responsible.
evidence: I have not killed anything.
Your house did, anyway

questions.prompt: Choose one detail of the Munchkins’ or the little woman’s clothes. What does it help you picture?
facilitatorNotes: Pointed hats with tinkling bells, the blue of the men’s clothes, the white gown sprinkled with stars. Each child can choose a different detail and say what sound or colour it adds.
evidence: little bells around the brims that tinkled sweetly

questions.prompt: What did Dorothy believe about witches, and how does the Witch of the North sort the four witches of Oz?
facilitatorNotes: Dorothy thought all witches were wicked. The Witch explains that North and South are good, East and West wicked, and that now only the Witch of the West remains wicked.
evidence: But I thought all witches were wicked
there is but one wicked Witch in all the Land of Oz

days.title: Oz, chapter II, part 2: silver shoes and a road of yellow brick
days.challenge: Keep track of what Dorothy is given and what she still does not know.
days.focus: Gifts, a message and a road set up the rest of the journey.
days.context: Recap: Dorothy’s house has landed in the country of the Munchkins and killed the Wicked Witch of the East. The good Witch of the North has told her there were four witches in Oz.
days.contentNote: The Witch of the North calls Kansas “civilized” and Oz not, meaning that Oz still has witches and wizards. The dead witch dries up in the sun, leaving only her shoes.

excerpt.locator: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (George M. Hill, 1900; PG 43936), chapter II, second part, to the end of the chapter; begins “"But," said Dorothy, after a moment's thought, "Aunt Em has told me”; ends “to disappear in just that way, and was not surprised in the least.”

questions.prompt: Why does the Witch of the North think Aunt Em was right that the witches were all dead?
facilitatorNotes: In “civilized countries” there are none left; Oz still has them because it is cut off from the rest of the world. Ask whether Dorothy’s Kansas facts are wrong or simply belong to a different place.
evidence: In the civilized countries I believe there are no witches left

questions.prompt: What does one Munchkin say about the silver shoes, and why might Baum leave that question unanswered here?
facilitatorNotes: There is “some charm” connected with them, but nobody knows what. An unanswered question gives listeners a reason to watch the shoes later.
evidence: there is some charm connected with them; but what it is we never knew

questions.prompt: How does the Witch of the North find out what Dorothy should do?
facilitatorNotes: She balances her cap on her nose, counts “one, two, three,” and the cap turns into a slate with a chalk message. She reads Dorothy’s name from it and only then asks it.
evidence: At once the cap changed to a slate

questions.prompt: What does Dorothy take with her from this chapter to protect or guide her?
facilitatorNotes: The Witch’s kiss, which leaves a shining mark; directions to follow the road of yellow brick to Oz; and the silver shoes, which she has carried into the house.
evidence: no one will dare injure a person who has been kissed by the Witch of the North
The road to the City of Emeralds is paved with yellow brick

days.title: Oz, chapter III excerpt: a welcome on the yellow road
days.challenge: Separate a community’s interpretation of someone from her own knowledge.
days.focus: Ordinary clothing becomes misleading evidence in a strange country.
days.context: Recap: the Witch of the North kissed Dorothy’s forehead and sent her to ask Oz, in the City of Emeralds, for help getting home; the road there is paved with yellow brick. Chapter III, “How Dorothy Saved the Scarecrow,” begins as soon as she is alone.
days.contentNote: The passage refers back to the Witch of the East’s death in chapter II.

excerpt.locator: Project Gutenberg 43936, 1900 George M. Hill text: Oz, chapter III excerpt: a welcome on the yellow road; begins “When Dorothy was left alone she began to feel hungry. So she went to the cupboard and cut ”; ends “the great Oz could help her get to Kansas again, so she bravely resolved not to turn back.”.

questions.prompt: Which preparations show Dorothy thinking about a long walk?
facilitatorNotes: She packs bread, changes clothes, and replaces worn shoes. These ordinary practical steps anchor the fantastic journey.
evidence: noticed how old and worn her shoes were

questions.prompt: Why does Boq think the checks on her dress prove she is friendly?
facilitatorNotes: Blue means Munchkins and white means witches in his local customs. Dorothy chose a clean dress, without intending that message.
evidence: Blue is the color of the Munchkins, and white is the witch color

questions.prompt: What changes Dorothy’s mood after the comfortable visit?
facilitatorNotes: Boq warns of a long journey and dangerous places; she worries but continues because she wants to reach Kansas.
evidence: she bravely resolved not to turn back

days.title: Oz, chapter III excerpt: meeting the Scarecrow
days.challenge: Compare what someone says they lack with what their actions already show.
days.focus: A new friendship begins with practical help and an uncertain promise.
days.context: After a night with Boq, Dorothy continues toward the Emerald City. She hopes Oz can send her home to Kansas.

excerpt.locator: Project Gutenberg 43936, 1900 George M. Hill text: Oz, chapter III excerpt: meeting the Scarecrow; begins “She bade her friends good-bye, and again started along the road of yellow brick. When she ”; ends “"No," answered the Scarecrow; "it's a lighted match."”.

questions.prompt: Why is lifting the Scarecrow easy for Dorothy but important to him?
facilitatorNotes: He is light because he is stuffed with straw, yet he cannot free himself from the pole. A small effort answers a big need.
evidence: for, being stuffed with straw, it was quite light

questions.prompt: Does Dorothy promise that Oz will give the Scarecrow brains?
facilitatorNotes: She says she cannot tell, invites him along, and promises only to ask. The friendship does not require pretending to know the result.
evidence: I cannot tell

questions.prompt: Why does the Scarecrow offer to carry the basket?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes an advantage of his straw body: he does not tire. Compare that useful ability with his distress over having a straw head.
evidence: I shall not mind it, for I can't get tired

days.title: Fancy and Fact
days.challenge: Notice the gap between a pretty picture and an uncomfortable experience.
days.focus: The narrator interrupts a romantic scene with practical consequences.
days.context: “Watteau dress” suggests an elegant painted pastoral scene. A flageolet is a small wind instrument; lumbago means back pain.
days.contentNote: The narrator attributes a cold and back pain to damp grass. This is a comic nineteenth-century explanation, not medical guidance.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “FANCY AND FACT”, beginning “O! a shepherd and a shepherdess,
  They dwelt in Arcadee,
And they wer”, ending “That the Poets often sing
Of those joys which in the practice
  Are another sort of thing.”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 78.

questions.prompt: Which details make the scene seem attractive at first?
facilitatorNotes: Dress, flowers, music, spring, and green grass build a pleasing picture.
evidence: With buds and blossoms set.

questions.prompt: What ordinary detail spoils that picture?
facilitatorNotes: The grass is damp and the two become uncomfortable or ill in the narrator’s account. The same dewy setting has a less attractive side.
evidence: the ground was damp,

questions.prompt: Does the final advice forbid enjoying poems?
facilitatorNotes: It asks readers to distinguish imagined pleasure from actual experience. We can enjoy an image while examining its omissions.
evidence:
those joys which in the practice
  Are another sort of thing.

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — tracks in the snow (opening scene)
days.challenge: Separate an observed footprint from the exciting explanations children invent.
days.focus: A familiar landscape becomes an adventure through the children’s imagination.
days.context: The narrator remembers a snowy childhood day with Charlotte. They leave a snowball game and begin exploring. This is the frame story around a tale they will later hear.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 1–10; begins “FOOTPRINTS in the snow have been unfailing provokers of sentiment ever since snow was firs”; ends “mudgy traces in the snow we were in a fair way to capture a half-grown specimen of a fabulous beast.”.

questions.prompt: Why do buttons and boot-laces suddenly seem badly designed to the children?
facilitatorNotes: Getting dressed delays their access to the waiting snow. The impatient description reflects their wishes rather than proving the fastenings are useless.
evidence: all that snow going to waste at our very door

questions.prompt: What does the white “garment” image suggest about the garden they already know?
facilitatorNotes: Snow covers familiar features so that the same world feels hidden and mysterious. Invite a drawing of familiar objects under a blanket-like layer.
evidence: our familiar world had so suddenly hidden itself

questions.prompt: What evidence supports Charlotte’s dragon idea, and what does she invent to explain an objection?
facilitatorNotes: She calls the marks lizard-like; when they seem too small, she proposes a young dragon. This is imaginative reasoning, not confirmation of a real dragon.
evidence: all dragons must be small to begin with

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — a book and a storyteller (frame-story scene)
days.challenge: Track the movement from uncertain tracks to a warm room and then an oral story.
days.focus: An adult respects children’s imagination without insisting their guess is true.
days.context: Charlotte and the narrator have decided that unfamiliar tracks may belong to a small dragon. They follow them beyond their own garden.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 11–24; begins “We ran the monster across the paddock and along the hedge of the next field, and then he t”; ends “So he thought a minute, and then he told us this story.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator less sure than Charlotte that they are still following real tracks?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary footprints mingle with them, and Charlotte seems determined to continue. His doubts distinguish observation from a fixed idea.
evidence: imagination and a fixed idea will do a great deal

questions.prompt: How does the circus-man offer a useful next step without mocking the dragon theory?
facilitatorNotes: He invites them to tea and to search his illustrated beast-book. He leaves room for a mistake while keeping their curiosity alive.
evidence: we'll try and find your beast in it!

questions.prompt: Why does the walk home feel different once the man joins them?
facilitatorNotes: The darkness had seemed eerie, but company makes the walk a treat and brings a story. Mood changes although the outside world remains dark.
evidence: a walk with a real Man

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — a family’s different kinds of knowledge (story scene)
days.challenge: Compare practical experience and book-learning without dismissing either.
days.focus: A family responds to frightening news by asking for an account before judging.
days.context: The circus-man begins a tale of a shepherd, his wife and their book-loving son. Here the father starts to describe a troubling discovery.
days.contentNote: The narrator mentions that some children might be cuffed; this family instead treats their child’s knowledge respectfully.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 25–32; begins “Long ago—might have been hundreds of years ago—in a cottage half-way between this village ”; ends “"Saw who?'' said his wife, beginning to share in her husband's nervous terror.”.

questions.prompt: What arrangement lets the parents and son contribute different kinds of knowledge?
facilitatorNotes: They provide practical knowledge while he reads books; the narrator calls this a fair division. Neither kind is presented as wholly useless.
evidence: they should supply the practical knowledge, and he the book-learning

questions.prompt: Why does the mother ask for the whole account before deciding what to do?
facilitatorNotes: She expects the three of them can understand it together. Her calm question slows the father’s fearful reaction.
evidence: tell us all about it first

questions.prompt: Which sounds make the father suspicious before he actually sees anything?
facilitatorNotes: Sighing, grunts and strange snoring emerge from the cave. Ask how sound creates suspense without a visible creature.
evidence: noises like heavy sighings

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — only a dragon (story scene)
days.challenge: Notice when a description of peaceful behaviour conflicts with a frightened label.
days.focus: The family’s reactions range from alarm to expertise to sympathy.
days.context: The shepherd has finally seen the creature near the cave. His wife and son listen to his description.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 33–38; begins “"Why him, I'm a telling you!" said the shepherd. "He was sticking half-way out of the cave”; ends “ut quick enough. He's got a pleasant sort o' way with him that makes everybody tell him everything."”.

questions.prompt: Which details show the creature is calm even in the frightened shepherd’s own account?
facilitatorNotes: It enjoys the evening, rests its chin on its paws and seems to meditate. The father admits it has behaved properly.
evidence: a peaceable sort o' beast enough

questions.prompt: Why does the word “only” startle the father?
facilitatorNotes: For the boy, identifying a dragon makes the situation ordinary within his book knowledge; for the father, the label is itself alarming.
evidence: It's only a dragon.

questions.prompt: What does the mother imagine the creature may need that the father has not considered?
facilitatorNotes: Supper and someone to talk with. She begins to think of loneliness and hospitality instead of only scales and claws.
evidence: without a bit o' hot supper or anyone to change the news with

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — an awkward first visit (story scene)
days.challenge: Use dialogue to follow two characters correcting their first assumptions.
days.focus: Friendship begins with boundaries, politeness and an admission of loneliness.
days.context: The boy walks up to the cave after tea to meet the dragon for himself.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 39–47; begins “Next day, after he'd had his tea, the Boy strolled up the chalky track that led to the sum”; ends “"You surprise me," said the Boy, civilly.”.

questions.prompt: What surprises the boy that his books did not tell him?
facilitatorNotes: The dragon purrs contentedly. His direct meeting adds information beyond what he has read.
evidence: None of my books ever told me that dragons purred!

questions.prompt: Why does the dragon begin with a list of things the boy must not do?
facilitatorNotes: He expects possible teasing or hurt. The boy objects to being treated as troublesome before he has done anything.
evidence: or bung stones, or squirt water

questions.prompt: How can the dragon be happy with his home and still welcome a visitor?
facilitatorNotes: He enjoys occupation and scenery but admits it can be dull. Contentment with a place does not remove the wish for company.
evidence: it is a trifle dull at times

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — poetry and a problem (story scene)
days.challenge: Hold together the dragon’s self-description and the reputation others may impose on him.
days.focus: Shared artistic interests create friendship, while stereotypes threaten it.
days.context: The dragon has admitted he is lazy and is explaining how he reached the cave. The boy stays to listen.
days.contentNote: Characters mention traditional dragons devouring people and villagers threatening this dragon. No attack occurs in this scene; the tale questions those expectations.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 48–66; begins “"It's the sad truth," the dragon went on, settling down between his paws and evidently del”; ends “ealise that you're a pestilential scourge, or you'll find yourself in a most awful fix. Good-night!"”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night carries, between “That’s just what I don’t precisely know,” and “said the dragon.”, the title “THE RELUCTANT DRAGON” and the quoted caption of Maxfield Parrish’s full-page plate (pp. 168–169 in the transcription); the library work grahame-dream-days-1902 leaves the plates and their captions out, as this record’s edition says, so the night is not a range of it. The story text otherwise agrees.

blocks.text: "It's the sad truth," the dragon went on, settling down between his paws and evidently delighted to have found a listener at last: "and I fancy that's really how I came to be here. You see all the other fellows were so active and earnest and all that sort of thing—always rampaging, and skirmishing, and scouring the desert sands, and pacing the margin of the sea, and chasing knights all over the place, and devouring damsels, and going on generally—whereas I liked to get my meals regular and then to prop my back against a bit of rock and snooze a bit, and wake up and think of things going on and how they kept going on just the same, you know! So when it happened I got fairly caught."
"When what happened, please?" asked the Boy.
"That's just what I don't precisely know,"
THE RELUCTANT DRAGON
"'What's your mind always occupied about?' asked the Boy.
'That's what I want to know.'"

said the dragon. "I suppose the earth sneezed, or shook itself, or the bottom dropped out of something. Anyhow there was a shake and a roar and a general stramash, and I found myself miles away underground and wedged in as tight as tight. Well, thank goodness, my wants are few, and at any rate I had peace and quietness and wasn't always being asked to come along and do something. And I've got such an active mind—always occupied, I assure you! But time went on, and there was a certain sameness about the life, and at last I began to think it would be fun to work my way upstairs and see what you other fellows were doing. So I scratched and burrowed, and worked this way and that way and at last I came out through this cave here. And I like the country, and the view, and the people—what I've seen of 'em—and on the whole I feel inclined to settle down here."
"What's your mind always occupied about?" asked the Boy. "That's what I want to know."
The dragon coloured slightly and looked away. Presently he said bashfully:
"Did you ever—just for fun—try to make up poetry—verses, you know?"

"Course I have," said the Boy. "Heaps of it. And some of it's quite good, I feel sure, only there's no one here cares about it. Mother's very kind and all that, when I read it to her, and so's father for that matter. But somehow they don't seem to—"

"Exactly," cried the dragon; "my own case exactly. They don't seem to, and you can't argue with 'em about it. Now you've got culture, you have, I could tell it on you at once, and I should just like your candid opinion about some little things I threw off lightly, when I was down there. I'm awfully pleased to have met you, and I'm hoping the other neighbours will be equally agreeable. There was a very nice old gentleman up here only last night, but he didn't seem to want to intrude."
"That was my father," said the Boy, "and he is a nice old gentleman, and I'll introduce you some day if you like."
"Can't you two come up here and dine or something to-morrow?" asked the dragon, eagerly. "Only, of course, if you've got nothing better to do," he added politely.

"Thanks awfully," said the Boy, "but we don't go out anywhere without my mother, and, to tell you the truth, I'm afraid she mightn't quite approve of you. You see there's no getting over the hard fact that you're a dragon, is there? And when you talk of settling down, and the neighbours, and so on, I can't help feeling that you don't quite realise your position. You're an enemy of the human race, you see!"
"Haven't got an enemy in the world," said the dragon, cheerfully. "Too lazy to make 'em, to begin with. And if I do read other fellows my poetry, I'm always ready to listen to theirs!"

"Oh, dear!" cried the Boy, "I wish you'd try and grasp the situation properly. When the other people find you out, they'll come after you with spears and swords and all sorts of things. You'll have to be exterminated, according to their way of looking at it! You're a scourge, and a pest, and a baneful monster!"

"Not a word of truth in it," said the dragon, wagging his head solemnly. "Character'll bear the strictest investigation. And now, there's a little sonnet-thing I was working on when you appeared on the scene—"

"Oh, if you won't be sensible," cried the Boy, getting up, "I'm going off home. No, I can't stop for sonnets; my mother's sitting up. I'll look you up to-morrow, sometime or other, and do for goodness' sake try and realise that you're a pestilential scourge, or you'll find yourself in a most awful fix. Good-night!"

questions.prompt: How does the dragon’s account of old dragon life distinguish him from the other dragons?
facilitatorNotes: He preferred meals, snoozing and thought rather than chasing or fighting. The contrast makes an individual out of a frightening type.
evidence: I liked to get my meals regular

questions.prompt: Why do the boy and dragon immediately understand each other when poetry is mentioned?
facilitatorNotes: Both make verses and feel listeners are kind but do not really appreciate them. Their unfinished explanations become a shared recognition.
evidence: my own case exactly

questions.prompt: What problem does the boy see that the dragon keeps trying to replace with poetry?
facilitatorNotes: People may attack him merely because he is a dragon. His good intentions do not automatically change their expectations.
evidence: You're an enemy of the human race

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — rumours and a hero (story scene)
days.challenge: Compare a rumour with the narrator’s explicit statement about what has actually happened.
days.focus: Crowd excitement can grow despite a lack of evidence for harm.
days.context: The boy and dragon have become friends, and the shepherd has met him. News of the dragon reaches the village.
days.contentNote: The villagers say the dragon should be killed; the narrator explicitly questions the accusations. No violence occurs in this scene.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 67–75; begins “The Boy found it an easy matter to set the mind of his parents at ease about his new frien”; ends “oured in after him. But the Boy made off up the hill as fast as he could lay his legs to the ground.”.

questions.prompt: What specific evidence undermines the villagers’ claim that the dragon is destroying their community?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says not even a hen roost has suffered. The dragon’s identity, rather than damage, drives their claim.
evidence: not even a hen-roost was the worse

questions.prompt: How can the villagers be frightened of the dragon and proud to have one at the same time?
facilitatorNotes: They regard him as a danger but also a distinction that makes their village special. Both feelings feed the talk.
evidence: a feather in the cap of the village

questions.prompt: Why is the boy’s reaction to St. George complicated?
facilitatorNotes: He admires the hero’s beauty and joins the cheering, yet soon runs to warn his dragon friend. Admiration for one does not erase concern for the other.
evidence: he found himself cheering with the rest

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — refusing the expected fight (story scene)
days.challenge: Distinguish wanting excitement from considering the cost to a friend.
days.focus: The dragon refuses a role that others think his identity requires.
days.context: St. George has arrived to confront the dragon. The boy rushes uphill with the news.
days.contentNote: The boy fears the dragon could be beheaded. This is a stated fear, not an injury scene; the dragon refuses to fight.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 76–85; begins “"It's all up, dragon!" he shouted as soon as he was within sight of the beast. "He's comin”; ends “terly to himself "The dragon treats the whole affair as if it was an invitation to tea and croquet."”.

questions.prompt: What is the dragon doing while the boy expects him to prepare for battle?
facilitatorNotes: He is polishing his scales with borrowed flannel. The calm domestic action contrasts comically with the alarm.
evidence: rubbing them with a bit of house-flannel

questions.prompt: Why does the boy initially think fighting is unavoidable?
facilitatorNotes: He treats the names St. George and dragon as fixed parts in a familiar story, and he wants the excitement. The dragon challenges that assumption.
evidence: cos he's St. George and you're the dragon

questions.prompt: What responsibility does the dragon place on the boy when he refuses?
facilitatorNotes: He asks the boy to arrange a solution and expresses complete confidence. The praise also shifts the hard work to his young friend.
evidence: I leave it entirely to you.

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — explaining “good” (story scene)
days.challenge: Notice that two speakers can use the same word with different meanings.
days.focus: A friend’s testimony challenges a heroic visitor’s assumptions.
days.context: The boy visits St. George privately, hoping to prevent a deadly confrontation.
days.contentNote: Accusations of violence and animal-baiting are discussed as unproved or wrongful; the passage depicts no such acts.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 86–96; begins “The villagers were straggling homewards as he passed up the street, all of them in the hig”; ends “ would, at hearing you talk in that—that loose way about matters on which he has very strong views!"”.

questions.prompt: When the boy calls his friend a good dragon, how does St. George first misunderstand “good”?
facilitatorNotes: The boy means kind; St. George thinks he means a strong opponent worthy of his weapon. Have two voices stress different words.
evidence: an adversary worthy of my steel

questions.prompt: What evidence about the villagers makes St. George begin to doubt their stories?
facilitatorNotes: The boy says they enjoy fights and are even betting on the dragon, despite praising the saint. The mismatch raises doubt about their motives.
evidence: betting six to four on the dragon

questions.prompt: Why does the boy object so strongly to the imagined captive princess?
facilitatorNotes: He knows the cave and his friend, whereas St. George is inventing a familiar dragon accusation. His distress shows the cost of assuming guilt from a type.
evidence: there's nothing of the sort in the cave at all

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — meeting before fighting (story scene)
days.challenge: Follow a negotiation in which each person wants something different.
days.focus: Conversation creates possibilities that a fixed heroic script had hidden.
days.context: After hearing the boy, St. George wonders whether he has misjudged the dragon. The boy proposes a visit.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 97–114; begins “"Well, perhaps I've been over-credulous," said St. George. "Perhaps I've misjudged the ani”; ends “ou can't want to have to go down that dirty old hole again and stop there till goodness knows when."”.

questions.prompt: Why is going to meet the dragon a more useful step than simply repeating stories about him?
facilitatorNotes: It gives St. George a chance to hear him directly and discuss the problem. The saint calls it sensible even though it breaks convention.
evidence: the most sensible thing to do

questions.prompt: What does the dragon say is missing from the proposed fight?
facilitatorNotes: Any actual disagreement or reason to fight. He calls the demand conventional and refuses to treat a role as a cause.
evidence: There's absolutely nothing to fight about

questions.prompt: Which appeal finally interests the dragon a little, and what earlier part of his character explains that?
facilitatorNotes: The beautiful visual picture of gold armour and blue scales appeals to his artistic sensibilities. It reaches the poet more than threats do.
evidence: Think what a picture it would make!

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — planning a harmless performance (story scene)
days.challenge: Separate the planned appearance of danger from the characters’ safety agreement.
days.focus: Negotiation includes asking what the supposedly defeated person will gain.
days.context: St. George and the dragon are discussing a staged fight instead of a real battle. The boy listens for fairness.
days.contentNote: A fantasy spear trick is planned as harmless within the story. It is make-believe, not an action to imitate.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 115–132; begins “"It might be arranged," said St. George, thoughtfully. "I must spear you somewhere, of cou”; ends “ of night. And my mother's sitting up, and do stop asking me to arrange more things till to-morrow!"”.

questions.prompt: Why does the dragon ask carefully whether St. George can find the agreed place?
facilitatorNotes: He would bear the injury if the saint made a mistake. Regret by the person holding the spear would not remove that risk.
evidence: you wouldn't regret it half as much as I should

questions.prompt: What question does the boy ask on the dragon’s behalf that changes the discussion?
facilitatorNotes: He asks what the dragon gains from losing. This brings the planned introduction to village society and banquet into view.
evidence: what are you going to get out of it?

questions.prompt: Why is the late request for a princess funny after all this practical arranging?
facilitatorNotes: St. George still remembers a story convention, while the exhausted boy has had enough tasks and needs home. No princess is actually arranged.
evidence: I can't arrange a Princess

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — the first round
days.challenge: Read a spectacle in two ways: what the crowd believes and what the boy knows.
days.focus: The dragon discovers an audience for performance rather than poetry.
days.context: The villagers think they will see a real battle; the Boy, the dragon and St. George know a performance has been arranged. This scene ends with the first round.
days.contentNote: The fight is staged; the crowd believes it is real.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 133–141; begins “Next morning the people began streaming up to the Downs at quite an”; ends “trust the dragon all right. What a regular play-actor the fellow is!"”

questions.prompt: Why do spectators choose places with a possible escape in mind?
facilitatorNotes: They do not know about the arrangement and fear what could happen if the dragon wins. Their seating reveals belief in real danger.
evidence: with a view to a speedy retreat

questions.prompt: What turns the boy’s worry about an absent dragon into admiration?
facilitatorNotes: The dragon emerges glittering, roaring and breathing fire with theatrical energy. The performance exceeds what the boy thought he could do.
evidence: What a regular play-actor the fellow is!

questions.prompt: St. George’s charge ends with the crowd yelling “Missed!” How do the crowd and the Boy understand that moment differently?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd thinks the saint has failed; the Boy sees a well-managed piece of acting. The same event looks different to people who know the plan.
evidence: "Missed!" yelled the crowd.
How well they managed it!

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — the second round
days.challenge: Follow how a crowd’s feelings change while the plan stays secret.
days.focus: The dragon enjoys being cheered, and St. George worries that success may spoil the plan.
days.context: Recap: before the whole village, St. George and the dragon have fought a first round that the Boy helped them plan in secret. The crowd believes the fight is real.
days.contentNote: The narrator compares the dragon’s whoops to a “Red Indian” and calls the Saint’s angry words to his horse an “Oriental flow of imagery.” Both phrases are stereotypes common in English writing when the story was published in 1898.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 142–150; begins “St. George had at last prevailed on his horse to stand steady, and”; ends “no telling where he would stop. I'll just finish him off this round."”

questions.prompt: What does St. George’s small three-finger signal tell the Boy that most spectators do not know?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests the third round is the planned finish. A tiny private gesture contrasts with the large public spectacle.
evidence: held up three fingers for an instant

questions.prompt: The narrator explains “ramping” as if teaching a dragon skill. Which words make the movement easy to picture?
facilitatorNotes: Running round in a wide circle and sending waves and ripples along the spine from the ears to the tail spike. Children can try the movement with their arms.
evidence: sending waves and ripples of movement along the whole length of your spine

questions.prompt: How does the crowd’s feeling about the dragon change during Round Two, and why?
facilitatorNotes: They begin to cheer him because he holds his own and clearly wants to “show good sport”; he struts about, enjoying it.
evidence: Round Two evoked audible evidence of friendly feeling towards the dragon.
hugely enjoying his new popularity

questions.prompt: Why does St. George decide to finish the fight in the next round, even though the Boy wants it to last?
facilitatorNotes: He fears the cheering has made the dragon conceited, so that he may forget the arrangement and play the fool. Some children think the saint is wise, others that he minds the dragon’s popularity; the text gives only his stated reason.
evidence: your simple-minded old friend's getting conceited
I'll just finish him off this round.

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — the third round and the welcome
days.challenge: Use a small gesture to interpret a scene that looks alarming at first.
days.focus: Public peace requires correcting rumours as well as ending a fight.
days.context: Recap: St. George and the dragon have fought two staged rounds. The crowd has begun cheering the dragon, and the Saint has told the Boy he will finish the fight in this third round.
days.contentNote: The staged spear scene looks dangerous but is explicitly painless. A spectator proposes further violence, which St. George declines.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 151–158; begins “He swung himself into the saddle and took his spear from the Boy. "Now don't you be afraid”; ends “rwards, won't you?" And the Boy always nodded, though he had promised his mother not to be out late.”.

questions.prompt: What reassures the boy that the fall is still a performance?
facilitatorNotes: The dragon opens an eyelid and winks, then plays collapsed again. The narrator confirms the agreed place was used.
evidence: winked solemnly, and collapsed again

questions.prompt: Which instruction in St. George’s speech protects another animal as well as the dragon?
facilitatorNotes: He orders the captive badger released and says he will check. The speech challenges the villagers’ appetite for animal fights.
evidence: a certain badger in the inn stables which had got to be released at once

questions.prompt: Do the saint, dragon, boy and villagers have exactly the same reason for enjoying the banquet?
facilitatorNotes: No: the saint avoided killing, the dragon gained acceptance, the boy kept both friends, and the crowd enjoyed the fight. Trace the repeated structure and differing motives.
evidence: his two friends were on the best of terms

days.title: The Reluctant Dragon — the long walk home (ending scene)
days.challenge: Recognize the return from a story inside a story to the children hearing it.
days.focus: Friendship includes practical care, and a carol lets imagination echo into ordinary life.
days.context: The staged fight has ended peacefully and the dragon has enjoyed his banquet. The tired boy still has a promise to keep. At the end, we return to Charlotte and the narrator walking home with their storyteller.
days.contentNote: The source ends with a traditional Christmas carol mentioning a dragon. After the banquet the dragon is too full and sleepy to walk home without help.

excerpt.locator: The Reluctant Dragon, Dream Days (1902), source paragraph indexes 159–177; begins “At last the banquet was over, the guests had dropped away with many good-nights and congra”; ends “that was the song, or something like it, that the dragon sang as he toddled contentedly up the hill.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night folds the closing carol (“Then St. George: ee made rev’rence…”) into one paragraph; the source prints it as four lines, which the library work grahame-dream-days-1902 keeps as a stanza, so the night is not a range of it. The words agree.

blocks.text: At last the banquet was over, the guests had dropped away with many good-nights and congratulations and invitations, and the dragon, who had seen the last of them off the premises, emerged into the street followed by the Boy, wiped his brow, sighed, sat down in the road and gazed at the stars. "Jolly night it's been!" he murmured. "Jolly stars! Jolly little place this! Think I shall just stop here. Don't feel like climbing up any beastly hill. Boy's promised to see me home. Boy had better do it then! No responsibility on my part. Responsibility all Boy's!" And his chin sank on his broad chest and he slumbered peacefully.

"Oh, get up, dragon," cried the Boy, piteously. "You know my mother's sitting up, and I 'm so tired, and you made me promise to see you home, and I never knew what it meant or I wouldn't have done it!" And the Boy sat down in the road by the side of the sleeping dragon, and cried.

The door behind them opened, a stream of light illumined the road, and St. George, who had come out for a stroll in the cool night-air, caught sight of the two figures sitting there—the great motionless dragon and the tearful little Boy.
"What's the matter, Boy?" he inquired kindly, stepping to his side.

"Oh, it's this great lumbering pig of a dragon!" sobbed the Boy. "First he makes me promise to see him home, and then he says I'd better do it, and goes to sleep! Might as well try to see a haystack home! And I'm so tired, and mother's—" here he broke down again.
"Now don't take on," said St. George. "I'll stand by you, and we'll both see him home. Wake up, dragon!" he said sharply, shaking the beast by the elbow.
The dragon looked up sleepily. "What a night, George!" he murmured; "what a—"

"Now look here, dragon," said the Saint, firmly. "Here's this little fellow waiting to see you home, and you know he ought to have been in bed these two hours, and what his mother'll say I don't know, and anybody but a selfish pig would have made him go to bed long ago—"

"And he shall go to bed!" cried the dragon, starting up. "Poor little chap, only fancy his being up at this hour! It's a shame, that's what it is, and I don't think, St. George, you've been very considerate—but come along at once, and don't let us have any more arguing or shilly-shallying. You give me hold of your hand, Boy—thank you, George, an arm up the hill is just what I wanted!"

So they set off up the hill arm-in-arm, the Saint, the Dragon, and the Boy. The lights in the little village began to go out; but there were stars, and a late moon, as they climbed to the Downs together. And, as they turned the last corner and disappeared from view, snatches of an old song were borne back on the night-breeze. I can't be certain which of them was singing, but I think it was the Dragon!
"Here we are at your gate," said the man, abruptly, laying his hand on it. "Good-night. Cut along in sharp, or you'll catch it!"
Could it really be our own gate? Yes, there it was, sure enough, with the familiar marks on its bottom bar made by our feet when we swung on it.
"Oh, but wait a minute!" cried Charlotte. "I want to know a heap of things. Did the dragon really settle down? And did—"
"There isn't any more of that story," said the man, kindly but firmly. "At least, not tonight. Now be off! Good-bye! "
"Wonder if it's all true?" said Charlotte, as we hurried up the path. "Sounded dreadfully like nonsense, in parts!"
"P'raps it's true for all that," I replied encouragingly.

Charlotte bolted in like a rabbit, out of the cold and the dark; but I lingered a moment in the still, frosty air, for a backward glance at the silent white world without, ere I changed it for the land of firelight and cushions and laughter. It was the day for choir-practice, and caroltime was at hand, and a belated member was passing homewards down the road, singing as he went:—

"Then St. George: ee made rev'rence: in the stable so dim, Oo vanquished the dragon: so fearful and grim. So-o grim: and so-o fierce: that now may we say All peaceful is our wakin': on Chri-istmas Day!"
The singer receded, the carol died away. But I wondered, with my hand on the door-latch, whether that was the song, or something like it, that the dragon sang as he toddled contentedly up the hill.

questions.prompt: Why does the boy compare seeing the dragon home to seeing a haystack home?
facilitatorNotes: The dragon is enormous and asleep; the task seems physically impossible for one tired child. The comparison makes his frustration concrete.
evidence: Might as well try to see a haystack home!

questions.prompt: How does St. George offer help without simply telling the boy to try harder?
facilitatorNotes: He says he will stand by him and they will both take the dragon home. He shares the burden and wakes the dragon.
evidence: we'll both see him home

questions.prompt: Why might the narrator connect the passing singer’s carol with the dragon’s song?
facilitatorNotes: Both concern St. George and a dragon; the sound crosses from the tale into the snowy real world. The narrator wonders rather than claiming proof that the story happened.
evidence: whether that was the song, or something like it

days.title: Bed-Time
days.challenge: Connect a repeated instruction with changing parts of the body.
days.focus: Small counting questions become a rhythm of settling to sleep.
days.context: “Jack Frost” is a personification of cold weather. An adult may ask each counting question and pause for a response.

excerpt.locator:
Bed-Time; source blocks 258–260, beginning “How many toes has the tootsey foot?
One, two, three, four, five.
Shut them all up in the l” and ending “ so shining and bright.
Shut them up under the little white lids.
And kiss them a loving good-night.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 69.

questions.prompt: Why does the hand’s answer say four and then add one?
facilitatorNotes: The poem distinguishes the thumb from the other four fingers while still counting five digits.
evidence: Four, and a little wee thumb.

questions.prompt: How are the toes like bees in this comparison?
facilitatorNotes: They are tucked closely into a safe, snug space. Toes do not literally become bees.
evidence: Snugger than bees in a hive.

questions.prompt: What changes about “shut them” in the last verse?
facilitatorNotes: Socks and bedclothes first cover body parts; eyelids finally close over eyes, bringing the poem to sleep.
evidence: Shut them up under the little white lids.

days.title: The Song of the Foolish Old Woman
days.challenge: Explain emotions by looking ahead to what a character expects.
days.focus: Anticipation reverses the apparent feelings of a hard and an easy journey.
days.context: The speaker watches a woman carrying a load up and down a hill. The title gives a judgment that readers can examine.

excerpt.locator:
Complete poem “Ye song of ye foolish old woman.”, beginning “I saw an old woman go up a steep hill,
And she chuckled and laughed, a”, ending “gh-ho! I am vexed,
     Because I expects,"
Says she, "I shall ache in climbing the next."”; plain-text transcription, author signature excluded. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 28.

questions.prompt: Why does the woman laugh on the difficult climb?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks ahead to reaching the top, so present strain is accompanied by hope.
evidence: At the top of the hill. He! he!

questions.prompt: Why does the easy descent fail to make her happy?
facilitatorNotes: She is already worrying about another climb rather than enjoying the easier road.
evidence: I shall ache in climbing the next.

questions.prompt: Would you call both of her ways of thinking foolish?
facilitatorNotes: Different answers are possible: looking forward can encourage effort, while constant worry can spoil relief. Compare the two scenes rather than simply accepting the title.
evidence: When you laughed, as you climbed up the hill-side so steep?

days.title: The Pencil and the Scratch Pad help (excerpt)
days.challenge: Keep track of who dreams, who writes, and how the writing tools move.
days.focus: A child’s apparent limitation becomes a shared imaginative project.
days.context: Jimmieboy is sleepy on his father’s lap while his mother reads about dream poetry. Mucilage is glue; a scratch pad is paper for rough notes. The tools’ movements belong to his fantasy.

excerpt.locator: III. Jimmieboy’s Dream Poetry; opening “If there is anything in the world that Jimmieboy likes better than custard and choo-c”; closing “ mamma was reading and papa's head was thrown back, so that his eyes rested on the picture moulding.”.

questions.prompt: What reason does Jimmieboy first give for being unable to write dream poetry? How does he answer himself?
facilitatorNotes: He does not yet know letters without picture clues, but argues that this is true only when he is awake. His own question and answer begin the imaginative possibility.
evidence: True; but that's only when I'm awake.

questions.prompt: Why need the Pencil and Pad not become sleepy themselves?
facilitatorNotes: They divide the task: Jimmieboy supplies sleep and dreams, while the tools handle writing. That solves the Pad’s objection.
evidence: Jimmieboy, does the sleeping and dreaming, and you and I do the rest.

questions.prompt: How is glue given an unusual helpful job?
facilitatorNotes: It slows the Pad’s slide from the desk so it can get down without a big jump. The author imagines a familiar sticky property doing new work.
evidence: The mucilage will keep you from going too fast.

days.title: Looking through the rock (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow a change from seeing a place to understanding how to enter it.
days.focus: A magical picture-world plays with what part of a person can travel.
days.context: Subterranean means underground. Jimmieboy is sitting on a familiar rock near a tennis court; a kaleidoscope makes changing patterns. This opening ends with an explanation of how his senses already reach the hidden place.

excerpt.locator: IV. A Subterranean Mutiny; opening “It seemed rather strange that it should have been left there, and yet Jimmieboy was g”; closing “"They are in now," said the other. "You can see me, you can hear me, and I can hear you."”.

questions.prompt: Before the rock turns transparent, what imaginative uses has Jimmieboy already made of it?
facilitatorNotes: It has been an island in a sea of grass and a seat from which to imagine himself umpiring. The magical event grows from a place already used for make-believe.
evidence: As a make-believe island in a raging sea of grass,

questions.prompt: How do the wall pictures differ from ordinary pictures even before the shepherd falls?
facilitatorNotes: Their people move, talk and play; the images keep changing. The falling shepherd makes that animated world reach beyond its frame.
evidence: they moved about, and talked, and romped

questions.prompt: When the shepherd says only part of Jimmieboy may enter, does he mean cutting him into pieces?
facilitatorNotes: No: he means sight, hearing and voice can reach the space although the rest of the body remains outside. The explanation turns a worrying literal idea into a joke about perception.
evidence: You can see me, you can hear me, and I can hear you.

days.title: The Dictionary corrects a camel (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish a useful correction from a deliberately silly comparison.
days.focus: An authoritative book becomes a teasing conversational character.
days.context: A dromedary is a one-humped camel; a milk dairy sells milk products. The talking Dictionary mixes a real fact with playful invented language.

excerpt.locator: V. Jimmieboy in the Library; opening “"I'm going to sit in this comfor'ble arm-chair by the fire," said Jimmieboy, climbing”; closing “respects in which the dromedary is like a base-drum—there isn't a solitary window in either of 'em."”.

questions.prompt: What would Jimmieboy like about his father having two humps, and what fact does the Dictionary correct?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines one seat for each brother, but a dromedary has only one hump. His wish is affectionate and practical within the joke.
evidence: one for me, and one for my little brother.

questions.prompt: Why does Jimmieboy rule out his father as the speaker? Is his reasoning reliable?
facilitatorNotes: His father claims he cannot do more than three things at once and is already doing three. The child applies that claim literally; readers need not accept it as a real limit.
evidence: he was now doing that many

questions.prompt: What unexpected shared feature connects the dromedary with a bass drum?
facilitatorNotes: Neither has a window. This technically true similarity is comically unhelpful as a way to identify a camel.
evidence: there isn't a solitary window in either of 'em.

days.title: Kingsway
days.challenge: Compare three offers of finery with the lady’s repeated choice.
days.focus: A repeated refusal separates outward splendour from being loved.
days.context: Kingsway is a London street name. A wimple is a head covering, a circlet a small crown, and duffle a thick cloth. Read the offers and the lady’s replies in two voices; the final Somebody is left unnamed.

excerpt.locator: Kingsway; complete poem, opening “Walking on the King's Way, lady, my lady,”, closing “And Somebody will kiss me and call me his queen.”.

questions.prompt: What stays the same when the offered colours change from red to blue to green?
facilitatorNotes: She keeps choosing grey duffle rather than bright colours and jewels. The repeated refusal establishes her own preference against the suggestions.
evidence: I will go in duffle grey

questions.prompt: Which details show that the suggested outfits are especially grand?
facilitatorNotes: Rubies, sapphires, emeralds, a golden girdle, and an ermine border suggest luxury. Ask for actual details rather than merely saying “fancy.”
evidence: With a golden girdle, and a pointed velvet slipper,
And a crown of emeralds fit for a queen?

questions.prompt: How does the last line give her a different way of being a queen?
facilitatorNotes: Someone will lovingly call her his queen without her wearing a crown or jewels. Accept readings about affection or personal choice, while noting that the person’s identity is not supplied.
evidence: And Somebody will kiss me and call me his queen.

days.title: The Conceited Apple-Branch — a flower judges its neighbours (part 1)
days.challenge: Distinguish the narrator’s account from the proud branch’s opinions about worth.
days.focus: A warm sunbeam supplies an alternative to a flower’s social ranking.
days.context: A beautiful apple branch is brought into a countess’s room. The plants and sunbeam speak as people do in this tale.
days.contentNote: The tale uses Christian language to express care for all creation. The branch’s disdain for supposedly low-ranking people and plants is a viewpoint the story challenges.

excerpt.locator: Hans Andersen’s Fairy Tales (Mrs. H. B. Paull, tr.; Frederick Warne, [1888]), “The Conceited Apple-Branch” (printed pp. 189–191), paragraphs 1–10 of the tale as transcribed from the page images; begins “THE CONCEITED APPLE-BRANCH.”; ends “really very thankful that I was not made like one of these flowers.””
excerpt.inlineReason: No full text of this Warne [1888] printing exists to cite: the only transcription linked to the scan (Wikisource) proved to be a different printing, and this night’s text was transcribed from the scan’s page images for its tale alone. The night stays inline until the whole book is transcribed from the page images.

blocks.text: THE CONCEITED APPLE-BRANCH.

It was the month of May. The wind still blew cold; but from bush and tree, field and flower, came the welcome sound, “Spring is come.” Wild-flowers in profusion covered the hedges. Under the little apple-tree, Spring seemed busy, and told his tale from one of the branches which hung fresh and blooming, and covered with delicate pink blossoms that were just ready to open. The branch well knew how beautiful it was; this knowledge exists as much in the leaf as in the blood; I was therefore not surprised when a nobleman’s carriage, in which sat the young countess, stopped in the road just by. She said that an apple-branch was a most lovely object, and an emblem of spring in its most charming aspect. Then the branch was broken off for her, and she held it in her delicate hand, and sheltered it with her silk parasol. Then they drove to the castle, in which were lofty halls and splendid drawing-rooms. Pure white curtains fluttered before the open windows, and beautiful flowers stood in shining, transparent vases; and in one of them, which looked as if it had been cut out of newly fallen snow, the apple-branch was placed, among some fresh, light twigs of beech. It was a charming sight. Then the branch became proud, which was very much like human nature.

People of every description entered the room, and, according to their position in society, so dared they to express their admiration. Some few said nothing, others expressed too much, and the apple-branch very soon got to understand that there was as much difference in the characters of human beings as in those of plants and flowers. Some are all for pomp and parade, others have a great deal to do to maintain their own importance, while the rest might be spared without much loss to society. So thought the apple-branch, as he stood before the open window, from which he could see out over gardens and fields, where there were flowers and plants enough for him to think and reflect upon; some rich and beautiful, some poor and humble indeed.

“Poor, despised herbs,” said the apple-branch; “there is really a difference between them and such as I am. How unhappy they must be, if they can feel as those in my position do! There is a difference indeed, and so there ought to be, or we should all be equals.”

And the apple-branch looked with a sort of pity upon them, especially on a certain little flower that is found in fields and in ditches. No one bound these flowers together in a nosegay; they were too common; they were even known to grow between the paving-stones, shooting up everywhere, like bad weeds; and they bore the very ugly name of “dog-flowers,” or “dandelions.”
“Poor, despised plants,” said the apple-bough, “it is not your fault that you are so ugly, and that you have such an ugly name; but it is with plants as with men,—there must be a difference.”

“A difference,” cried the sunbeam, as he kissed the blooming apple-branch, and then kissed the yellow dandelion out in the fields. All were brothers, and the sunbeam kissed them—the poor flowers as well as the rich.

The apple-bough had never thought of the boundless love of God, which extends over all the works of creation, over everything which lives, and moves, and has its being in Him; he had never thought of the good and beautiful which are so often hidden, but can never remain forgotten by Him,—not only among the lower creation, but also among men. The sunbeam, the ray of light, knew better.
“You do not see very far, nor very clearly,” he said to the apple-branch. “Which is the despised plant you so specially pity?”

“The dandelion,” he replied. “No one ever places it in a nosegay; it is often trodden under foot, there are so many of them; and when they run to seed, they have flowers like wool, which fly away in little pieces over the roads, and cling to the dresses of the people. They are only weeds; but of course there must be weeds. Oh, I am really very thankful that I was not made like one of these flowers.”

questions.prompt: Which special treatment helps the apple branch begin thinking it is more important than other plants?
facilitatorNotes: The countess shelters it with a silk parasol and places it in a fine vase. These details explain its pride without proving it deserves higher worth.
evidence: sheltered it with her silk parasol

questions.prompt: Why does the branch call the dandelion ugly even though it has hardly looked at its shape?
facilitatorNotes: It points to the common name, abundance, and places it grows. Its judgment rests on status and familiarity rather than careful observation.
evidence: they were too common

questions.prompt: How does the sunbeam answer the branch before making a speech?
facilitatorNotes: It kisses both blossoms. Its equal action gives a visible answer to the branch’s claim that one is superior.
evidence: the sunbeam kissed them—the poor flowers as well as the rich

days.title: The Conceited Apple-Branch — another kind of loveliness (part 2)
days.challenge: Collect three different reasons for valuing the same overlooked flower.
days.focus: Pleasure, usefulness and beauty each challenge a narrow judgment.
days.context: The apple branch has called the dandelion worthless. A sunbeam now asks it to watch children, an older woman and the countess.
days.contentNote: Blowing seeds to predict new clothes is a children’s belief inside the story, not a reliable prediction. Religious language belongs to the original tale.

excerpt.locator: Hans Andersen’s Fairy Tales (Mrs. H. B. Paull, tr.; Frederick Warne, [1888]), “The Conceited Apple-Branch” (printed pp. 189–191), paragraphs 11–20 of the tale as transcribed from the page images (end of the tale); begins “There came presently across the fields a whole group of children, the”; ends “the blooming apple-branch, upon whose leaves appeared a rosy blush.”

blocks.text: There came presently across the fields a whole group of children, the youngest of whom was so small that it had to be carried by the others; and when he was seated on the grass, among the yellow flowers, he laughed aloud with joy, kicked out his little legs, rolled about, plucked the yellow flowers and kissed them in childlike innocence. The elder children broke off the flowers with long stems, bent the stalks one round the other, to form links, and made first a chain for the neck, then one to go across the shoulders, and hang down to the waist, and at last a wreath to wear round the head, so that they looked quite splendid in their garlands of green stems and golden flowers. But the eldest among them gathered carefully the faded flowers, on the stem of which was grouped together the seed, in the form of a white feathery coronal. These loose, airy wool-flowers are very beautiful, and look like fine snowy feathers or down. The children held them to their mouths, and tried to blow away the whole coronal with one puff of the breath. They had been told by their grandmothers that whoever did so would be sure to have new clothes before the end of the year. The despised flower was by this raised to the position of a prophet or foreteller of events.
“Do you see,” said the sunbeam, “do you see the beauty of these flowers? do you see their powers of giving pleasure?”
“Yes, to children,” said the apple-bough.

By-and-by an old woman came into the field, and, with a blunt knife without a handle, began to dig round the roots of some of the dandelion-plants, and pull them up. With some of these she intended to make tea for herself; but the rest she was going to sell to the chemist, and obtain some money.

“But beauty is of higher value than all this,” said the apple-tree branch; “only the chosen ones can be admitted into the realms of the beautiful. There is a difference between plants, just as there is a difference between men.
Then the sunbeam spoke of the boundless love of God as seen in creation, and over all that lives, and of the equal distribution of His gifts, both in time and in eternity.
“That is your opinion,” said the apple-bough.

Then some people came into the room, and, among them, the young countess,—the lady who had placed the apple-bough in the transparent vase, so pleasantly beneath the rays of sunlight. She carried in her hand something that seemed like a flower. The object was hidden by two or three great leaves, which covered it like a shield, so that no draught or gust of wind could injure it, and it was carried more carefully than the apple-branch had ever been. Very cautiously the large leaves were removed, and there appeared the feathery seed-crown of the despised yellow dandelion. This was what the lady had so carefully plucked, and carried home so safely covered, so that not one of the delicate feathery arrows of which its mist-like shape was so lightly formed, should flutter away. She now drew it forth quite uninjured, and wondered at its beautiful form, and airy lightness, and singular construction, so soon to be blown away by the wind.

“See,” she exclaimed, “how wonderfully God has made this little flower. I will paint it with the apple-branch together. Every one admires the beauty of the apple-bough; but this humble flower has been endowed by Heaven with another kind of loveliness; and although they differ in appearance, both are the children of the realms of beauty.”
Then the sunbeam kissed the lowly flower, and he kissed the blooming apple-branch, upon whose leaves appeared a rosy blush.

questions.prompt: What do the children make that changes ordinary flower stems into something splendid?
facilitatorNotes: They link stems into chains and a wreath. The pleasure comes from making and wearing, rather than from a rare or costly flower.
evidence: garlands of green stems and golden flowers

questions.prompt: Does the branch accept the dandelion after seeing it give pleasure and useful roots?
facilitatorNotes: No; it dismisses children’s pleasure and says beauty is higher than usefulness. Track how it keeps moving its reason for rejection.
evidence: But beauty is of higher value than all this

questions.prompt: Why does the countess’s careful covering of the seed-head matter to the final rosy blush?
facilitatorNotes: She protects it even more carefully than the branch and plans to paint both. The branch is confronted with admired beauty in what it despised; the blush may suggest embarrassment or a dawning change.
evidence: another kind of loveliness
